title: Where Is God When It Hurts: Suffering and the Goodness of God
subtitle: A five-session study on the problem of evil, the providence of God, and the hope that does not disappoint.
summary:
This study is for the person who has stood at a hospital bed, or a graveside, or in the wreckage of a marriage or a diagnosis, and asked the oldest question there is. If God is good, and God is able, why this. It is for the skeptic who left the faith over a child's cancer ward and was never given an answer worth the name, and for the Christian still inside the faith carrying a question the church kept handing them platitudes for. It is for the pastor who has run out of things to say at funerals. It does not promise to solve the problem of evil, because no honest book ever has, and the ones that pretend to are the ones that wound. It promises something harder and more durable. It takes the objection at its full and terrible strength, refuses every cheap answer, and walks toward the only response Scripture finally gives, which is not an argument but a Person who entered the suffering himself.

The five sessions move in order. First the question stated without flinching, the way the honest atheist states it, so well that the believer in the room feels it too. Then the doctrine of providence held without tidy resolution, a God who permits what he hates and works it toward an end we cannot see from inside it. Then the book of Job, where God answers the sufferer not with an explanation but with a whirlwind and a thousand questions, and rebukes the friends who had the formula. Then the cross, where the God who permits suffering does not stay outside it but enters it, bleeds inside it, dies inside it. And finally the hope that does not explain suffering away but defeats it, the resurrection and the new creation where every tear is wiped from every face. Bell does not write this from a safe distance. He came to God from atheism, and the problem of evil was the wall he could not get over for years. He has buried people he loved and prayed for healing that did not come. He is not solving a puzzle for you. He is standing in the rubble with you, pointing at the only light he has found that the dark could not put out.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: The Question That Will Not Quiet
sessions.aim: To state the problem of evil at its full strength, in the form its most honest unbelievers give it, before reaching for any answer, so that the room feels the genuine weight of the objection rather than a straw version of it, and so that no one is handed a comfort that has not first looked the horror in the face.
sessions.summary: Every other session in this study depends on this one being honest, so we begin by refusing the cheap answer. The problem of evil is the oldest argument against God and the strongest, and it is not strong because clever atheists invented it. It is strong because it rises off the maternity ward and the cancer floor and the mass grave, off the suffering of a child who did nothing to deserve it. The first question is not how to answer it. The first question is whether we will state it truthfully. Bell takes the objection in its hardest form, the form Dostoevsky put in the mouth of Ivan Karamazov, who does not deny God but says that if the price of the world's final harmony is the unavenged tears of one tortured child, he respectfully returns his ticket. He grants the full force of it, because he lived inside it. The problem of evil was the wall he could not climb for years, the reason he stayed an atheist. He will not insult the suffering in the room by reaching too fast for a verse. He names the three claims that cannot all be true at once, that God is all-good, all-powerful, and that evil is real, and he refuses to dissolve the problem by quietly dropping one of them. The turn of this first session is not an answer. It is a posture. The God of the Bible never scolds the sufferer for asking. The Psalms ask it. Job asks it. Jesus, on the cross, asks it. So the question is not the enemy of faith. The question is permitted to be as large as it actually is, and the study begins by letting it be that large.

keyScripture.why: How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever. How long will you hide your face from me. The Bible's own prayer book opens the question of God's apparent absence in suffering without rebuke, modeling that the cry of the afflicted is permitted to be as honest as the pain, and that faith begins not by silencing the question but by being allowed to ask it of God himself.

discussion.q: Before any theology, name the honest version. When you have watched real suffering, the kind that seems senseless and undeserved, what is the question it raised in you, and did you feel allowed to ask it?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the real question, not the polite one. Most people have carried it and felt they were not supposed to. The aim is to let the question be spoken at its true size and to establish, from the first minute, that asking it is permitted. Go first if the room is slow, and do not rush to answer anything yet.

discussion.q: Bell takes the objection at full strength, the way Ivan Karamazov does, refusing a happy ending that is bought with the unavenged suffering of even one tortured child. Where do you feel the force of that, and is there a part of you that thinks the objection is right?
discussion.behind: Press the room to feel the steelman, not to defeat it. The point of the session is that the objection is genuinely strong. Help people admit that it lands, even for believers, because a faith that cannot feel the weight of this question has not understood it. Resist the urge to resolve it here.

discussion.q: The three claims in tension are that God is all-good, that God is all-powerful, and that evil is real and terrible. Cheap answers quietly drop one of them. Where have you heard someone resolve the problem by secretly letting go of one of the three?
discussion.behind: Get the room to name the cheap moves. God is not really able. Evil is just an illusion or a lesson. God is not really good, just powerful. The aim is to see that each easy answer survives only by abandoning something the Bible refuses to abandon, which is why the honest problem stays hard.

discussion.q: What is the worst answer you have ever been given, or have given, to someone in real grief, the kind that wounded instead of helped? Why do you think we reach for those answers so quickly?
discussion.behind: Expose the tendency to fix pain with formula. Everything happens for a reason, God needed another angel, at least. The aim is honest recognition that we hand out cheap answers mostly to relieve our own discomfort with the silence, and that the sufferer almost always feels it as a second wound. Handle gently, some will recognize their own words.

discussion.q: Bell admits the problem of evil was the wall he could not climb for years, the reason he stayed an atheist. Where is your own faith most honestly pressed by suffering, and have you ever brought that pressure to God instead of around him?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, including the leader. The aim is not to manufacture doubt but to let the room admit that this question presses on real faith, and that bringing it to God is itself an act of faith. The skeptic in the room should feel met here, not managed. Go first and keep it honest.

objections.objection: If God is all-powerful he could stop the suffering of innocent children, and if he is all-good he would want to. He does not. So either he cannot, in which case he is not the God you preach, or he will not, in which case he is not good. There is no third option, and every answer I have ever heard is just a way of refusing to admit it.
objections.response: This is the argument at its strongest, and Bell will not pretend it is weak, because it is not, and dressing it down would be the first dishonesty. He stood on this side of it for years. So hear what the study will and will not do with it. It will not dissolve the problem by quietly dropping one of the three claims, because the Bible drops none of them. God is good. God is able. Evil is real and it is hateful, and Scripture never once calls a murdered child a teaching moment. What the study denies is that those three exhaust the possibilities, that the only options are an impotent God or a cruel one. There is a third thing the argument cannot see from where it stands, which the rest of this study walks toward, that a good and able God might permit, for a time, an evil he hates, for the sake of an end that requires the permission and that he does not leave us alone inside. That is not a proof, and Bell will not pretend it is. It is a claim that the dilemma is not as airtight as it looks, offered by someone who once found it airtight and no longer does, and not because the suffering got smaller.

objections.objection: You are going to give me an intellectual answer to a wound. My grief is not a debate I lost. Even if you constructed a logically airtight theodicy, it would not raise the dead or unburn the child, and the fact that you are reaching for argument at all proves you do not understand what suffering actually is.
objections.response: You are right, and this is the most important thing said in the whole first session, so do not let it pass. An argument does not heal a grave. If this study ended in a clever proof, it would have failed, because the problem of evil is not finally a problem to be solved but a wound to be entered, and the Bible knows this better than the philosophers do. Notice that God's own answer to the worst sufferer in Scripture, Job, was not a syllogism. It was his presence and a flood of questions that explained nothing. Notice that the deepest word the Bible speaks into suffering is not an argument at all but a cross, God himself inside the pain. So the study begins with the intellectual question because honesty demands we state it plainly, but it does not end there, and it never claims that the answer to grief is a better paragraph. The answer the Bible gives is a Person who entered the dark, and you are not wrong to refuse anything less.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the suffering, yours or someone you love, that has most pressed on whether you can believe God is good, and have you ever said that to God in as many words?
sessions.practice: This week, do not try to answer the question. Sit with it honestly instead. Once, take the suffering that presses hardest on your faith, the loss or the diagnosis or the senseless thing, and bring it to God in prayer not as something to apologize for but as the psalmists do, plainly, how long, why, where are you. Do not tidy it. Do not end on a forced note of resolution. If you are not sure God is there, say that too. Write down what it was like to bring the question to God instead of carrying it around him, and whether being permitted to ask changed anything about how heavy it felt.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we are not going to pretend tonight. Some of us have seen things that do not fit any tidy story, and we have been told to hush about them, and we have hushed, and the question only went underground and grew. We bring it up tonight, out loud, where you can hear it. If you are good and you are able, why the child, why the cancer, why the silence. We do not have the answer and we will not manufacture one. But we have noticed that you do not scold the ones who ask. Your own book is full of the question. So we ask it, and we trust that asking it to your face is closer to faith than swallowing it ever was. Stay with us as we look at this honestly. Do not let us settle for an answer too small for the wound. Amen.
reflection: What is the cheap answer I am most tempted to reach for when someone is suffering, and whose discomfort is it actually meant to relieve, theirs or mine?
Which of the three claims, God's goodness, God's power, the reality of evil, am I quietest about letting go of when the problem gets too heavy, and what does that reveal?
Have I ever felt that asking God the hard question was a failure of faith, and what would change if I believed, as the Psalms suggest, that asking it is an act of faith?
sessions.teaching: We are going to begin this study by doing the one thing most studies on suffering refuse to do, which is to state the problem honestly before we say a single comforting word, because every comfort that has not first looked the horror full in the face is a lie, and the suffering in this room can smell that lie from across the table. So here is the question, in its oldest and hardest form. If God is perfectly good, he must want to end suffering. If God is all-powerful, he must be able to end suffering. Suffering has not ended, and not the suffering of villains getting what they earned, but the suffering of children who did nothing, of the faithful who prayed and got silence, of whole peoples ground into the dirt. Therefore, the argument runs, either God is not good, or God is not able, or one of those words does not mean what you say it means. This is not a trick invented by hostile professors. It is the cry that goes up off every cancer ward and every battlefield and every nursery where a small casket had to be built, and it is old. The philosopher Epicurus framed a version of it three centuries before Christ. It has never been answered to everyone's satisfaction, and I am going to tell you now, plainly, that I am not going to answer it to yours either, because if I could reduce the suffering of the world to a paragraph that made it all make sense, that paragraph would be obscene. I want to take this objection at its full strength, in the form a great novelist gave it, because the form matters. In Dostoevsky's novel The Brothers Karamazov, published in 1880, there is a character named Ivan, and Ivan is not a fool and not a villain. He is the honest unbeliever, and he says something that has haunted the faith ever since. Ivan does not argue that God does not exist. He says something worse. He says that even if there is a God, and even if at the end of all things there is a perfect harmony where everything is reconciled and every wrong made right, he cannot accept it, because the price of that harmony is too high. The price includes the unavenged tears of tortured children, suffering that no future bliss can justify or undo. And so, Ivan says, with great respect, he returns his ticket. He will not buy a paradise built on that. Now hear me. I am a Christian pastor, and I am telling you that Ivan's objection is the strongest thing said against God in modern literature, and that I do not think it is stupid, and that for years I agreed with it. Because I did not come to faith inside the church. I came to God out of atheism, and the wall I could not climb, for a long time, was this exact wall. I could not square the God I was being offered with the world I could see. And I want the skeptic in this room, the one who came tonight braced for a sales pitch, to hear that I am not going to pretend the wall is a small thing. It is not. So before we go one inch further, let us be precise about why the problem is so hard, because the cheap answers all work the same way. There are three claims here. God is all-good. God is all-powerful. Evil is real and it is terrible. The reason the problem will not quiet is that all three appear to be true and they appear to collide. And almost every easy answer you have ever been handed survives by quietly letting go of one of them while pretending it has not. Some say God is not really able, that he would help if he could but his hands are tied, and they have traded the God of the Bible for a sympathetic weakling. Some say evil is not really real, that it is an illusion, or a lesson, or a stage of growth, and they have stood in front of a grieving mother and called her dead child a teaching tool. Some say God is powerful but not really good in any sense we would recognize, that he has his reasons and they are simply above morality, and they have made God a tyrant we obey out of fear. Each of these dissolves the problem by amputating a limb of the truth, and the reason the honest problem stays hard is that the Bible refuses every one of those amputations. Scripture insists God is good, all the way good. It insists he is sovereign, all the way able. And it never, not once, softens the horror of evil into something acceptable. The Bible weeps at gravesides. It does not lecture. So we are left holding three things that will not fit, and I am not going to make them fit by cheating tonight. But here is the first thing I want you to actually take home, and it is not an answer, it is a posture, and it changes everything about how the rest of this study will go. The God of the Bible does not punish the sufferer for asking the question. We have somehow gotten the idea that the faithful response to suffering is to swallow the question, to clamp down on the why, to perform a serenity we do not feel, as though God were fragile and our honesty might offend him. Open the actual book. The Psalms, the prayer book God gave his own people, are full of the question, raw and unedited. How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me. That last one is not the cry of a faithless man. It is Psalm 22, and it is the line Jesus chose to pray from the cross. Think about that. In the deepest agony in the history of the world, the Son of God reached not for a serene affirmation but for the Bible's own question, the why. The book of Job, which we will spend a whole session inside, is one long protest, a righteous man demanding an audience with God to ask what he did to deserve this, and at the end of it God is angry, but not at Job. He is angry at Job's friends, the ones who defended him with tidy theology. So here is the verdict that this first session leaves you with, and it is meant to leave you lighter, not heavier. The question is not the enemy of faith. The question is permitted to be exactly as large as the suffering that gave rise to it, and bringing it to God, to his face, in all its weight, is not the failure of faith but one of its truest acts, because you do not argue with someone you have given up on. You do not cry out to a God you are sure is not there. The atheist returns his ticket and walks away. The believer, sometimes, returns his ticket and stays in the room, shaking it at the God he has not stopped speaking to. We are going to stay in the room. We are going to let the question be as big as it really is. And we are going to walk slowly, across these five weeks, toward the only answer I have ever found that the dark could not put out, which is not a paragraph and not a proof, but a God who climbed down into the dark himself and has not left it. Tonight, we just name the question. Next week, we begin to ask what it could possibly mean that a good and able God permits what he hates.

scriptureStudy.note: How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever. The Bible's own prayer book opens with the question of God's apparent absence, and it is not rebuked, which means the cry of the afflicted is a permitted and even modeled form of faith, not its failure.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me. The cry of dereliction, and the verse Jesus prayed from the cross, which means the why of the sufferer was taken up by the Son himself and carried into the heart of God.

O Lord, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear. The prophet brings the problem of unanswered injustice directly to God as a complaint, and God answers him, modeling that the protest belongs inside the relationship, not outside it.

Why did I not die at birth. Job, called blameless by God himself, voices the rawest possible despair, and the book does not condemn him for it, distinguishing honest anguish from the sin of cursing God.

My soul is bereft of peace, I have forgotten what happiness is, so I say my endurance has perished. Scripture preserves the words of a man who has lost hope, refusing to airbrush suffering, before any turn toward mercy comes.

Why does the way of the wicked prosper. The prophet brings the oldest form of the problem, the prospering of evil and the suffering of the faithful, as a direct question to a God he has not stopped trusting.

Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just. Abraham presses God on the justice of his dealings, and God receives the challenge, showing that the demand for God to be good is itself something Scripture honors.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long history of the problem of evil, because seeing how old and how serious it is guards the room from treating it as a modern complaint to be swatted away. The earliest sharp framing comes down to us through Epicurus, roughly three centuries before Christ, in the form later writers preserved, the dilemma of a God either unwilling or unable to prevent evil. The eighteenth-century philosopher David Hume gave it its most famous modern statement, and in the twentieth century the problem was sharpened into what philosophers call the logical and the evidential forms, the first claiming the existence of evil is strictly incompatible with a good and all-powerful God, the second claiming that the sheer quantity and apparent pointlessness of suffering makes such a God improbable. A serious group should know that the philosopher Alvin Plantinga is widely credited with showing that the strict logical contradiction does not hold, that there is no formal inconsistency in an all-good, all-powerful God permitting evil for a sufficient reason, which is why most who press the problem today press the evidential form, the felt weight of pointless suffering rather than a proof. But the study insists on something the philosophers can miss, that the deepest form of the problem is not the argument but the wound, and that Dostoevsky's Ivan, in The Brothers Karamazov, voices it more honestly than any syllogism, because Ivan grants the logic might work and still returns his ticket, refusing a reconciliation purchased by the tears of a tortured child. Set the logical relief beside the existential weight and ask which one actually keeps people awake. The discipline of this session is to hold both, to know that the airtight contradiction does not hold while refusing to let that abstract relief stand in for the real comfort, which the rest of the study locates not in an argument at all but in the God who entered the suffering himself.

sessions.title: The God Who Permits
sessions.aim: To hold the doctrine of providence honestly, that a good and sovereign God permits what he hates and works it toward an end we cannot see from inside it, without the tidy resolution that turns evil into something acceptable, and to name plainly where the mystery genuinely remains rather than papering over it.
sessions.summary: Having stated the question at full strength, we turn to what Scripture actually claims about God and the things that happen, and the claim is harder and stranger than either the skeptic or the comfortable believer expects. The Bible does not teach a God who is helpless before evil, nor a God who authors it, but a God who permits what he hates and bends it, against its own intent, toward an end. The first question is whether that is coherent or just a dodge. Bell takes the strong form of the suspicion, that permits is a weasel word, that an all-powerful God who permits a thing he could have stopped is as responsible as one who caused it, so the word changes nothing. He grants the force of it. He will not pretend providence is a clean machine where every horror has a visible purpose, because Scripture does not say that and saying it has wounded countless sufferers. But he holds up the verdict the Bible does give, in the mouth of Joseph, sold into slavery by his own brothers and raised to save them, who says of the evil done to him, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good. Two intentions, real evil and real good, running through the same event, and Joseph names both without collapsing either. The brothers' evil was genuine evil, not a disguised blessing. God's good was genuine good, not a justification of the evil. The turn is this. Providence is not the claim that everything that happens is good, or that we can read God's purpose off the surface of our suffering. It is the claim that no evil escapes God's reach, that even what is meant for harm can be made to serve an end its author never intended, and that this is true even when, especially when, we cannot see the end at all. The session ends by naming honestly the mystery that remains, that this side of heaven we are usually Joseph in the pit, not Joseph on the throne, and the verse is spoken in hindsight that we are rarely given in the moment.

keyScripture.why: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. Joseph names two real intentions running through one event, genuine evil done by his brothers and genuine good worked by God, without softening the evil into a blessing or reducing God's good to a mere permission, the closest thing Scripture gives to a doctrine of providence stated by a sufferer himself.

discussion.q: Scripture says God permits evil he hates. Be honest about the suspicion. Does permits sound to you like a real distinction, or like a word we use to keep God's hands clean while he could have stopped it and did not?
discussion.behind: Open by naming the objection directly rather than assuming the room accepts the word. The aim is to feel the genuine difficulty in permits before any answer, so the room does not receive a glib distinction it has not earned. Hold the suspicion long enough that it is real, then move toward Joseph.

discussion.q: Joseph says to the brothers who sold him, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good. He names both, real evil and real good, in one breath. Why does it matter that he does not collapse one into the other?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel the two intentions held together. The brothers' act was evil, not a disguised kindness. God's good was real, not a justification of the evil. The aim is to see that providence does not baptize the evil as secretly good, which is the cheap move, but insists God can bend even genuine evil toward an end.

discussion.q: Joseph speaks that verse from the throne, years later, looking back. In the pit, and in the prison, he did not have it. Where are you, the pit or the throne, and what does it do to the verse to remember it was spoken in hindsight?
discussion.behind: This is the pastoral hinge. We quote Genesis 50:20 to people still in the pit as though they should already see the good. The aim is to feel that the verse is hindsight, a testimony Joseph could only give later, and that demanding sufferers produce it in the moment is cruelty dressed as faith. Handle tenderly.

discussion.q: There is a difference between saying God works good out of evil and saying the evil was therefore good, or necessary, or a blessing in disguise. Where have you seen that line crossed, and what damage did it do?
discussion.behind: Press on the line that protects the sufferer. Romans 8:28 says God works for good, not that all things are good. The aim is to expose the false comfort that calls the cancer a gift or the abuse part of God's plan, and to see that providence never requires us to call evil good.

discussion.q: Bell admits he cannot read God's purpose off the surface of most of his own suffering and refuses to pretend he can. Where have you felt pressure, from others or yourself, to produce a tidy reason for a loss, and what would it free you to admit you cannot see it?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication and honesty about mystery. The aim is to release people from the burden of manufacturing meaning they do not have, and to feel that admitting we cannot see the purpose is not a failure of faith but an honest form of it, trusting the God we cannot currently read.

objections.objection: Permits is a meaningless distinction. If I watch a man drown a child in a shallow pool and do nothing when I could easily have stopped it, no court on earth lets me off because I only permitted it. An all-powerful God who permits what he could prevent is as guilty as one who does it. You are hiding behind a word.
objections.response: Bell grants that the word, used carelessly, becomes exactly the dodge you describe, and he will not use it carelessly. So hear the actual claim, because it is not that permission makes God innocent of caring about the suffering, but that there is a category your courtroom example leaves out. The bystander at the pool gains nothing, intends nothing, and has no power to redeem the death he allows, which is precisely why we condemn him. The claim of providence is not that God idly watches, indifferent, but that he permits only what he is able to weave toward an end that could not come another way and that he himself enters and bears. That is a different thing from the bystander, who is merely absent. Whether it is enough is a fair fight, and Bell will not pretend the question is closed, because from inside the suffering it often does not feel like enough. But the analogy fails at the one point that matters, that the God of the Bible is not the man standing dry beside the pool. He is, as the rest of this study will show, the One who climbs into the water.

objections.objection: Joseph got a happy ending. He could say God meant it for good because he ended up running Egypt and saving his family. Most suffering does not resolve like that. The child still dies, the marriage still ends, and there is no throne at the end where it all makes sense. Joseph is a survivor telling a survivor's story, and survivors always think it worked out.
objections.response: This is the most honest objection to Genesis 50, and Bell will not wave it away, because most of us live in the pit chapters, not the throne chapter, and the Bible knows it. So notice what the study does not claim. It does not claim that every sufferer will be handed Joseph's hindsight, a clear view of the good their suffering served. Many will not, this side of death, and to promise otherwise is to lie. What Joseph's verse establishes is not that you will see the resolution but that there is a kind of God who can work one, that evil is not the final author of your story even when you cannot read the next chapter. Job never got an explanation. Paul's thorn was never removed. The claim is not you will understand, it is the reach of God is longer than the reach of the evil done to you, and the throne chapter, for the Christian, may lie on the far side of the resurrection rather than on this side of the grave. That is a harder hope than Joseph's, and an honest study has to say so.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where in your life have you been told to find the good in a loss before you were ready, and what would it mean to let God hold the meaning of it for now, even unseen?
sessions.practice: This week, take one hard thing in your past, far enough back that you can look at it with some distance, and do two things with it, in order. First, name the evil or the loss as real, plainly, without rushing to redeem it, refusing to call it secretly good. Then, only after that, ask honestly whether you can see any way God has brought any good out of it since, not to justify it but to trace his reach. If you can see it, give thanks for the good without ever blessing the evil. If you cannot see it, say so to God, and leave the meaning in his hands rather than manufacturing one. Write down which it was, and what it was like to hold the evil and the hope without collapsing either into the other.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we have been handed a hard thing tonight, that you permit what you hate, and we do not fully understand it, and we are not going to pretend we do. We confess we have used the word providence as a club, telling broken people to find the good before they could even breathe. Forgive us. Teach us to be like Joseph, who looked at the brothers who sold him and called their act evil to its face, and in the same breath trusted that you had been at work in it for good. Where we are still in the pit, and many of us are, give us the patience to leave the meaning with you, unseen, rather than forcing one we do not have. We trust not that we can read your purpose, but that you are good and your reach is long. Amen.
reflection: Where am I tempted to call an evil secretly good in order to feel better about it, when Scripture only ever claims God can work good out of it without making it good?
Am I in the pit or on the throne right now, and have I been demanding of myself a hindsight verse I have not been given yet?
What would it free in me to admit that I cannot currently see God's purpose in a particular suffering, and to leave the meaning of it in his hands rather than my own?
sessions.teaching: Last week we let the question be as large as it really is, and we refused every cheap answer that survives by quietly amputating one of the three claims. Tonight we have to ask what the Bible actually says about God and the things that happen, and I have to warn you up front that the biblical answer is stranger and harder than either side usually expects. The skeptic expects the Bible to teach a tyrant who decrees every horror, and many Christians have unfortunately preached exactly that. The comfortable believer expects a God who is always intervening to stop the bad things, and then is bewildered when he does not. Scripture teaches neither. It teaches a God who permits what he hates, and bends it, against its own intent, toward an end. And the first honest thing to say is that the moment I use the word permits, a sharp objection should rise in your throat, and if it does not, you are not paying attention. Permits sounds like a dodge. If a man stands beside a shallow pool and watches a child drown when he could have reached in and pulled the child out, we do not let him off because he merely permitted it. We charge him. So an all-powerful God who permits what he could have prevented seems, at first, to be in exactly that position, and to say he only permitted it seems like hiding behind a word to keep God's hands clean. I want to grant the full force of that, because it is a serious objection and a glib answer to it would betray everything we said last week. But I want to show you why the analogy, powerful as it is, fails at the one point that turns out to matter most, and to do that I am going to take you to the clearest thing the Bible says about how evil and the purpose of God run through the same event, which is the story of Joseph. Here is a man sold into slavery by his own brothers out of jealousy, lied about, imprisoned for years on a false accusation, forgotten in a dungeon. There is no way to read that as anything but a series of genuine evils done to an innocent man. And then, through a chain of events no one designed, Joseph rises to become the second most powerful man in Egypt, positioned to save the entire region, including his own family, from a famine that would have wiped them out. Years later the brothers stand before him, terrified, certain he will finally take his revenge. And Joseph says one of the most important sentences in the whole Bible on this subject. You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. Now I want you to see exactly what Joseph does and does not say, because everything hangs on the precision of it. He does not say, what you did was not really evil, it was secretly a blessing. He looks at his brothers and calls their act what it was. You meant evil. The selling was evil. The lying was evil. The years stolen from his life were a real theft. He does not soften any of it into a disguised kindness. And in the very same breath, without erasing a word of the first half, he says God meant it for good. Two intentions, running through one event. The brothers intended harm and accomplished harm. God intended good and accomplished good, and the good God worked was real, the saving of many lives. Joseph holds both, and he collapses neither. This is the heart of what the church has called providence, and notice how carefully it has to be stated, because the cheap version ruins it. The cheap version says everything that happens is good, or is God's perfect will, or is secretly for the best, and that version has stood in front of grieving mothers and called their dead children part of a plan, and it is a doctrine that wounds. That is not what Joseph says. The Apostle Paul writes the famous line in Romans, that for those who love God all things work together for good, and people misquote it constantly to mean that all things are good. Read it again. It does not say all things are good. It says God works in all things toward good, which is the Joseph claim exactly. The evil stays evil. God's reach into it, bending it toward an end its author never intended and never could have intended, is the good. So here is why the man beside the pool is the wrong picture of God, even though the objection is a strong one. The bystander at the pool gains nothing, intends nothing, and crucially has no power to redeem the death he allows. He is simply absent and indifferent, which is exactly why we condemn him. The God of providence is not absent and not indifferent. He permits only what he is able to weave toward an end that could not come another way, and, as the rest of this study will show, he does not stand dry at the edge of the water. He climbs in. The bystander watches the child drown. The God of the cross drowns with us, and pulls us up on the far side of death. Now I have to be honest with you about where this leaves us, because if I stop here it will sound tidier than it is, and tidiness is the enemy. Joseph speaks that verse from the throne. He says it years later, looking back, with the whole shape of the story finally visible. But for all the years in between, in the pit, in the slave market, in the dungeon, he did not have the verse. He could not see the good. He had no idea that the betrayal was positioning him to save nations. From inside it, it was just betrayal and loss and the slow grind of injustice with no visible point. And this is the thing we get wrong almost every time. We take a hindsight verse and shove it at people still in the pit, and we tell them to find the good now, today, in the fresh wound, as though faith meant producing Joseph's throne-room serenity from inside the dungeon. That is not faith. That is cruelty wearing faith's clothes. The honest truth is that most of us, most of the time, are in the pit chapters, not the throne chapter, and many sufferings in this life never get their Genesis 50, never resolve into a visible good we can point to and say, there, that was the reason. I cannot read God's purpose off the surface of most of my own suffering, and I am not going to stand here and pretend I can. I have buried people I loved and prayed for healing that did not come, and I do not have a clean account of what good it served, and I refuse to invent one to make myself feel better, because inventing one would be a lie and the people who love those I lost would smell the lie. So here is the verdict, and it is meant to be both harder and freer than the easy version. Providence is not the promise that you will understand. It is not the promise that you will be handed Joseph's hindsight this side of the grave. It is the claim that no evil, however real, however unredeemed it looks from the pit, escapes the reach of a God who is able to bend even what was meant for harm toward an end its author never intended. The reach of God is longer than the reach of the evil done to you. And where you cannot see the end, and often you will not, the faithful thing is not to manufacture a meaning you do not have. It is to leave the meaning with the God you cannot currently read, the way Joseph trusted in the pit before he understood on the throne. We are still missing the deepest thing, though, and you can feel it. Even a God who can work good out of evil can sound, from inside the dungeon, like a God who is managing your suffering from a comfortable distance. The Bible's final word on this is not management from a distance. It is a God who climbs into the pit himself. But before we get to the cross, we have to spend a week with the one man in Scripture who demanded an explanation to his face, and with the strange and staggering way God answered him, which was not to explain at all.

scriptureStudy.note: You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good. Joseph names two intentions in one event, real evil by the brothers and real good by God, the clearest scriptural statement of providence and the model for holding both without collapsing either.

We know that for those who love God all things work together for good. The verse says God works toward good in all things, not that all things are good, which guards against the cheap reading that calls the suffering itself a blessing.

This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. The cross itself is the supreme case, a genuine evil done by guilty men that God worked toward the salvation of the world, both held at once.

My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the Lord. God names the gap between his purposes and our sight, which grounds the honesty that we often cannot read his reasons from inside our suffering.

The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord. Job confesses God's sovereignty over his loss without claiming to understand it, holding trust and unanswered grief together before any explanation is given.

The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us. Scripture itself draws a line between what God has disclosed and what he has not, permitting us to leave the unseen purpose with him rather than inventing one.

Though he cause grief, he will have compassion, for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men. Even where God is named as permitting grief, Scripture insists it does not come from his heart, that he does not delight in the suffering he allows.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the distinction the older theologians drew between God's permission and his causation, because it is the hinge of this session and it has been argued for centuries with more care than the modern conversation usually brings. The Reformed tradition, following the broad stream of Augustine, has often spoken of God ordaining whatsoever comes to pass while at the same time being in no way the author of sin, holding divine sovereignty and human responsibility together as a tension to be confessed rather than a contradiction to be dissolved. Other faithful traditions, including much of the Arminian and Wesleyan stream, have laid greater weight on a genuine permission grounded in the freedom God grants his creatures, arguing that love requires the real possibility of its refusal. A serious group should state both in their strongest form and notice that this is a genuinely open question among faithful Christians, a place where the creeds bind us to God's goodness and sovereignty but do not settle the exact mechanism by which he relates to evil. The study lands closer to the language of permission, that God permits what he hates and bends it toward an end, because that language best preserves both his goodness and the reality of the evil, but it does not pretend the deepest mechanism is fully visible, and it grants that a thoughtful Christian holding the stronger sovereignty view has a real biblical case the study has not fully answered. Set this beside the warning of Deuteronomy 29:29, that the secret things belong to the Lord, and the discipline becomes clear, to confess what Scripture confesses, God's goodness, his sovereignty, the reality of evil, while refusing to claim a clarity about the inner workings of providence that Scripture itself withholds. The error in both directions is the same, a tidiness that resolves the mystery by quietly dropping something the Bible holds.

sessions.title: Job and the Whirlwind
sessions.aim: To sit inside the one book of Scripture that refuses the formula, where a blameless man suffers without cause and God answers him not with an explanation but with his presence and a flood of questions, and to feel the rebuke God lays on the friends whose tidy theology defended God by accusing the sufferer.
sessions.summary: The Bible has a whole book devoted to the problem of evil, and the most important thing about it is what it refuses to do. Job is a blameless man, and God says so out loud, and then Job loses everything, his children, his wealth, his health, for reasons Job is never told. The first question is what we expect the book to do, because we expect it to end with an explanation, and it does not. Bell takes the strong form of the reader's frustration, that God shows up at the end and never once tells Job why, never mentions the wager in heaven, never explains the suffering, just overwhelms him with questions about the foundations of the earth and the wild goat and the storehouses of the snow. He grants how unsatisfying that can feel. But he holds up what the book is actually doing, which is dismantling the formula that every one of us reaches for, the formula Job's friends preach for thirty chapters, that suffering is the punishment for sin, so if you are suffering you must have sinned. The friends defend God by accusing Job, and at the end God is furious, not with Job, but with them, because they have spoken what is not right about him. The man who shook his fist and demanded an audience is vindicated. The men who handed out tidy theology are rebuked. The turn is this. God's answer to suffering is not an argument but an encounter. He does not give Job a reason. He gives Job himself, and that, strangely, is enough, because Job says I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. The session ends by naming what the whirlwind does and does not give. It does not give an explanation. It gives a God who is present, and questions that put the sufferer back inside a universe too large to be reduced to his accounting, which is not a brush-off but a mercy.

keyScripture.why: Then the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind and said, who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge. Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth. God answers the sufferer not with an explanation of his suffering but with his presence and a flood of questions that restore Job to a universe larger than his own accounting, refusing the formula and giving an encounter where we expected an argument.

discussion.q: Job is the Bible's whole book on suffering, and God never tells Job why he suffered. What did you expect the book to do, and how do you sit with the fact that it withholds the explanation we most want?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the expectation the book refuses. We come to Job for the answer and leave without it. The aim is to feel that the withholding is deliberate and meaningful, not a gap, and to begin asking why God would answer a sufferer with presence rather than explanation.

discussion.q: Job's friends preach that suffering is punishment for sin, so Job must have done something. It sounds pious, even biblical. Where have you heard that formula, in others or in your own head, and what does it do to a sufferer?
discussion.behind: Expose the formula because we all carry it. The friends are not cartoon villains, they say things that sound true and are even quoted elsewhere in Scripture. The aim is to see how the formula, applied to the innocent sufferer, becomes a cruelty, and how naturally we reach for it to make suffering feel controllable.

discussion.q: At the end God is angry, not at Job who shook his fist, but at the friends who defended God with tidy theology. Why do you think God vindicates the protester and rebukes the explainers?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel the reversal. We assume the faithful response is serene acceptance and that the friends, who never cursed God, are the safe ones. God says the opposite. The aim is to see that honest protest to God's face is counted as faith, and that defending God by accusing the wounded is what he calls speaking wrongly about him.

discussion.q: God answers Job with questions about the foundations of the earth and the wild things, not with reasons. How is being put back inside a universe too large for your accounting a comfort rather than a brush-off?
discussion.behind: Help the room feel the whirlwind as mercy, not dismissal. The questions are not God belittling Job but enlarging him, restoring him to a creation he is part of but does not run. The aim is to see that sometimes the relief is not an explanation but a recovered sense of being small inside something vast and good.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has been all three at once, the sufferer, the friend handing out formulas, and the one who needed presence more than answers. Where have you been Job's friend, defending God by explaining someone else's pain, and what did it cost them?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. We have all been the friend, certain we were helping, handing the wounded a formula. Go first. The aim is honest recognition that the impulse to explain another's suffering is often about our own need for control, and that presence is almost always what the sufferer actually needed.

objections.objection: God's answer to Job is a cosmic power play. A man in unbearable grief asks a fair question, why is this happening to me, and God responds by listing his own credentials and asking if Job can make it rain on the desert. It is not an answer, it is intimidation, the biggest one in the room shutting up the smallest by sheer size.
objections.response: Bell grants that read coldly, the speech can sound like that, and a flippant teacher would skip right past the difficulty. So read it more closely, because the tone is not what it first seems. God does not actually condemn Job for asking. At the very end of the book God says Job spoke rightly about him, while the friends, who never questioned God, spoke wrongly, which is the reverse of a power play silencing dissent. What the whirlwind does is not crush Job but relocate him. It takes a man who has shrunk the entire universe down to the size of his own case, his own ledger of innocence and grievance, and it widens the frame until he is standing again inside a creation of staggering scale and wildness and beauty that he did not make and does not run. That is not God saying how dare you ask. It is God saying you are part of something far larger than your accounting of it, and the not-knowing you are suffering under is the not-knowing of a creature, not the abandonment of an orphan. Job does not come away crushed. He comes away saying now my eye sees you, which is the language not of a beaten man but of a met one.

objections.objection: Even if presence is the answer, that only works if you actually get the encounter. Job got a literal voice from a whirlwind. I have prayed in my own catastrophe and gotten nothing, no voice, no presence, just silence. So the book solves Job's problem by giving him an experience I have asked for and not received.
objections.response: This is the fair and painful question, and Bell will not pretend everyone gets a whirlwind, because they do not. So notice two things the book itself protects. First, Job did not get the encounter on demand or on schedule, he got it after chapter upon chapter of silence, after his friends had exhausted their formulas and his own protests had run dry, which means even in the book the presence comes late and through a long darkness, not as a quick fix. Second, the book of Job is itself given to us so that we would have, in advance, what Job did not, the knowledge that the formula is false, that the innocent do suffer, that God vindicates the honest protester, and that the deepest answer is presence. We are not promised a voice from a storm. But Christians are pointed beyond Job to a fuller presence than Job ever got, a God who did not speak from a whirlwind but entered the suffering in person, which is next week. If the silence is your present reality, the book does not shame you. It tells you the silence is not the verdict, and that the One who finally answered Job has since come closer than a voice from a cloud.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Have you ever, like Job's friends, defended God by explaining someone else's suffering, and what might it have given them instead if you had simply sat with them in it?
sessions.practice: This week, do two opposite things on purpose. First, find one person who is suffering and practice being the opposite of Job's friends, sit with them, listen, and resist every urge to explain their pain or hand them a reason. If you say almost nothing, you have done well. Second, for your own suffering, read Job 38 through 41 slowly, out loud if you can, and instead of looking for an answer, let the questions about the sea and the stars and the wild animals put you back inside a creation larger than your own case. Notice whether being made small inside something vast feels like a dismissal or, strangely, like a comfort. Write down what it was like to give presence instead of answers, and to receive presence instead of an explanation.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we came to Job for an answer and you gave us a whirlwind, and we are still learning that the whirlwind was the mercy. We confess that we have been the friends more often than the sufferer, certain we were defending you when we were only wounding the wounded, handing out tidy reasons to people who needed us to sit down and shut up and stay. Forgive us. Teach us the strange thing this book teaches, that you would rather have our honest fists than our false serenity, that you vindicated the man who argued and rebuked the men who explained. Where we are suffering, we are not asking tonight for the reason. We are asking for you. Put us back inside a world too large for our accounting, and let it be enough to know that the One who laid the foundations of the earth has not lost track of us. Amen.
reflection: Where do I carry the friends' formula, the quiet belief that suffering means someone must have sinned, and how has it made me a worse comforter and a harder sufferer?
Why does God vindicate Job's honest protest and rebuke the friends' careful theology, and what does that tell me about what God actually wants from me in my pain?
When have I needed presence more than an explanation, and have I been willing to give that to others, or do I rush to explain because the silence makes me uncomfortable?
sessions.teaching: There is a whole book of the Bible devoted to the question we have been asking, and the most important thing about it is what it stubbornly refuses to do. The book of Job opens by telling us something the rest of the book then withholds from Job himself, that Job is a blameless and upright man, a man God himself points to with something like pride, and that the catastrophe about to fall on him has nothing whatever to do with any sin. He has done nothing wrong. And then, in the space of a single terrible day, he loses everything. His livestock, his servants, and then, in the blow that empties the world, all ten of his children, killed when the house collapses. Later his health goes too, and he sits in ashes, scraping his sores with a piece of broken pottery, a man who had everything and now has nothing and does not know why. And hold onto this as we go. Job never finds out why. The reader is let in on the heavenly scene at the start, but Job is not, and Job goes to his grave, inside the book, never having been told the reason for what happened to him. Now we come to Job expecting it to end with the explanation, because that is what we want from any account of suffering, the reason that makes it bear up, and I want to take seriously how frustrating it is that the book refuses to give it. God does eventually show up, at the end, in a storm, and you lean in, finally, here it comes, the answer. And God does not give one. He does not mention the wager. He does not explain the suffering. He does not say, Job, here is what this was all for. Instead he asks Job questions, dozens of them, for four chapters, and they are not the questions you expect. Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth. Have you commanded the morning since your days began. Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades. On and on, a torrent of questions about the sea and the stars and the storehouses of the snow and the wild beasts no man can tame. Not one word of explanation for Job's loss. And the honest reader thinks, that is not an answer. I want to sit in that frustration with you, because it is real, and then I want to show you what the book is actually doing, because it is doing something far deeper than the explanation we wanted. To see it, you have to look at the friends. For the long middle of the book, Job's three friends sit with him, and at first they do the only truly wise thing in the whole book, they sit in silence for seven days because they see his suffering is very great. But then they open their mouths, and out comes the formula. God is just. God rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked. Therefore suffering is the punishment for sin. Therefore, Job, if you are suffering like this, you must have sinned, and the faithful thing for you to do is to confess it. They say it gently at first and then with mounting force, and the awful thing is that what they say sounds pious. It sounds biblical. Pieces of it are even quoted approvingly elsewhere in Scripture. They are defending God. They will not let Job impugn the moral order of the universe. And Job, who knows he has not earned this, refuses their formula and does something that ought to shock us. He demands an audience with God, says he wants to argue his case to God's face, shakes his fist at heaven, accuses God of treating him unfairly. He does not curse God and die, which his wife suggested and which would have been the end of his faith, but he does something the friends would call blasphemous, he brings his rage and his confusion straight to God and demands an answer. And now here is the hinge of the entire book, the thing that should rearrange how you think about all of this. When God finishes his whirlwind of questions, he turns to the friends, and he is angry. Not at Job. At them. He says to the chief of them, my anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has. Read that again and let it land. The men who defended God, who never questioned him, who handed out careful orthodox theology about sin and punishment, God says they spoke wrongly about him. And the man who argued, who protested, who shook his fist and demanded an explanation, God says he spoke rightly. The protester is vindicated. The explainers are rebuked, and God makes them go to Job and ask Job to pray for them, which must have been a bitter cup. So what was wrong with the friends. It was not that they were unkind, at least not at first, and it was not that everything they said was false. It was that they took a formula that works in general, that sin has consequences, and weaponized it against an innocent man in agony, and in doing so made God smaller than he is and made Job's suffering his own fault. They defended God by accusing the wounded. And God will not have it. He would rather have Job's honest, furious, faithful protest than the friends' tidy, orthodox, cruel explanation. Now go back to the whirlwind, because once you see the friends rebuked, it reads completely differently. It is not God doing to Job what the friends did, crushing him with superior force. It takes a man who, in his agony, has shrunk the entire universe down to the size of his own case, his own ledger of innocence and grievance, until the whole cosmos is just the courtroom of Job versus God. And God, by asking about the foundations of the earth and the wild goat and the chains of the Pleiades, gently and overwhelmingly enlarges the frame. He puts Job back inside a creation of staggering scale and wildness and beauty, full of things that have nothing to do with Job at all, things God delights in for their own sake. He is not saying how dare you ask. He is saying, my child, you are part of something far larger and wilder and more beautiful than your accounting of it, and the not-knowing you are suffering under is the not-knowing of a creature inside a vast good creation, not the abandonment of an orphan in an empty universe. And here is the proof that this is mercy and not a brush-off. Job is not crushed by it. He comes away saying something astonishing. I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. He got no explanation, none, and yet he says he has been given something better than he had before. He had known about God. Now he has seen God. The encounter was the answer. Not an argument. A presence. So here is the verdict this strange and magnificent book leaves us with. God's deepest answer to suffering is not a reason. It is himself. He did not give Job an explanation, and he very often will not give you one, and the book of Job is in the Bible partly to free you from the friends' lie that you must have done something to deserve it and partly to free you from the demand that God owes you an explanation before you will trust him. What God gives instead is his presence, and the strange testimony of those who have suffered deeply and met him in it is that it is enough, not because it answers the question but because it dissolves the loneliness underneath the question, which was always the worst part. And I have to put myself in this honestly, because I have been all three people in this book. I have been Job, raging at a silence I could not understand. I have needed presence far more than an answer, and gotten it, late, after long dark. And God help me, I have been the friends, sitting across from someone in real agony and handing them a formula, certain I was defending God when I was only adding to their wound, because their suffering made me uncomfortable and an explanation let me feel like I had it under control. We are all the friends more often than we admit. The book is a warning to every one of us who has ever rushed to explain another person's pain. Sit down. Be quiet. Stay. Give them your presence, which is the only thing God himself gave Job, and stop defending God, who is perfectly able to defend himself and would rather have your honest grief than your false serenity. We have come a long way. We have stated the question at full strength, seen that God permits what he hates and bends it toward an end we usually cannot see, and now seen that his answer to the sufferer is not an explanation but his presence. But there is one more thing, the deepest thing, and it is the thing Job never got to see. Job heard a voice from a storm. We have seen something more. We have seen the God who did not stay outside the suffering, shouting answers from a whirlwind, but climbed all the way down into it, into a body, into the dark, onto a cross. That is next week, and it is the center of everything.

scriptureStudy.note: Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man. God himself declares Job innocent before the suffering begins, which demolishes the friends' formula in advance and establishes that the righteous do suffer without cause.

They sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great. The friends' wisest act is their silent presence, before they ruin it by speaking, which models that being with the sufferer outranks explaining to them.

Though he slay me, I will hope in him, yet I will argue my ways to his face. Job holds trust and protest together, refusing both to curse God and to accept the friends' false formula, the very posture God later vindicates.

The Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind, who is this that darkens counsel, where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth. God answers with presence and questions, not explanation, relocating Job inside a creation larger than his own case.

I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. Job's response to the encounter, not the satisfaction of an explanation but the deeper rest of having seen God, which the book offers as the truest answer to suffering.

My anger burns against you and your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has. God rebukes the tidy theology of the friends and vindicates the honest protest of Job, reversing our assumptions about faithful suffering.

They showed him sympathy and comforted him for all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him. The narrator names the suffering as evil even while attributing it to God's permission, holding the reality of the evil and God's sovereignty together without resolving the tension.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the way the book of Job functions as a deliberate dismantling of what scholars call the doctrine of retribution, the ancient and widespread assumption that prosperity is the reward of righteousness and suffering the punishment of sin. This assumption runs through much of the wisdom literature in its ordinary form, that wise and righteous living tends toward flourishing, and there is real truth in it. Job is placed in the canon precisely to mark the limit of that truth, to insist that when the formula is turned into an iron law and applied to the innocent sufferer it becomes a lie and a cruelty. A serious group should notice that the friends quote sound theology, much of what they say would be unobjectionable in another setting, which is exactly what makes the book so unsettling, that true statements can be deployed falsely against a suffering person. Set this beside the Gospel of John, where Jesus is asked about a man born blind, who sinned, this man or his parents, the very logic of Job's friends, and Jesus refuses the question entirely, answering that it was not that this man sinned or his parents, breaking the retribution formula as decisively as the book of Job does. The discipline here is double. First, to surrender the secret retribution arithmetic we nearly all carry, the quiet sense that our suffering must be punishment and another's must be deserved. Second, to recover the wisdom of presence over explanation, to learn from the friends' failure that the call of the comforter is not to account for the suffering but to share it, and from the whirlwind that God's own deepest answer to the sufferer was not a reason but an encounter, a relocation of the wounded soul inside a creation and a Creator too large to be reduced to the sufferer's own accounting, which is not a dismissal of the question but the beginning of its healing.
