sessions.title: The Crucified God
sessions.aim: To arrive at the center of the Christian answer to suffering, that the God who permits suffering did not stay outside it but entered it himself, in a body, in agony, on a cross, so that the deepest word God speaks into human pain is not an explanation shouted from a safe distance but a presence bleeding inside it.
sessions.summary: Every religion and philosophy has to do something with suffering, and most of them keep their god at a distance from it, untouched, serene, above the fray. The Christian claim is the strange one, the offensive one, the one that changes everything, that the God who permits suffering climbed down into it himself. The first question is what difference that makes, because a God who suffers does not, on its face, solve the logical problem of evil any better than a God who does not. Bell grants that. A crucified God is not a tighter argument. But he holds up what it does answer, which is the deeper wound underneath the argument, the loneliness, the sense that we suffer in an empty universe under the gaze of a God who watches from a comfortable height and feels nothing. Christianity says no. The cross is God himself entering the worst of it, the betrayal, the injustice, the physical agony, the abandonment, even the cry of dereliction, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, the very question of this whole study prayed by God in human flesh. Bell takes the strong form of the skeptic's reply, that a suffering God is just a literary consolation, a sad story we tell ourselves so we do not feel alone, with no power to actually fix anything. He grants it has no power to fix the logic. But Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison before his execution, said that only the suffering God can help, that the God who is with us is the God who forsakes us, that the Bible directs us not to a god of power in the world but to the powerless and suffering God who alone can be beside us. The turn is this. The cross does not explain your suffering. It does something the explanation could never do. It tells you that whatever pit you are in, God has been there before you, not as a tourist but as one of the crucified, and that you do not suffer alone, and that the suffering is therefore not the last word, because the One who entered the grave walked back out of it.

keyScripture.why: He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows, the prophetic portrait of a God who does not stand above human suffering but takes it into himself, fulfilled at the cross where God in human flesh entered the betrayal, the injustice, the agony, and the abandonment, so that the deepest word God speaks into pain is not a reason but his own presence inside it.

discussion.q: Most pictures of God keep him serene and untouched, above suffering. The Christian claim is that God entered it, on a cross. When you sit with that, that God himself suffered, what does it stir, and is it a comfort or a scandal to you?
discussion.behind: Open on the strangeness of a crucified God. For some it is the most moving thing in the faith, for the skeptic it can seem absurd or weak. The aim is to surface the honest reaction and to begin feeling that a God who enters suffering is a different kind of God than the distant watcher most people assume.

discussion.q: On the cross Jesus prays the question of this whole study, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me. What does it do to your own why to know that God in human flesh prayed it too?
discussion.behind: Connect the cry of dereliction to the room's own questions. The point is that the why of session one is not foreign to God, he prayed it himself. The aim is to feel that the question is not outside the faith but at the very center of it, taken up into God, which means the sufferer asking it is in the deepest company.

discussion.q: The skeptic says a suffering God is just a sad story we tell ourselves so we do not feel alone, with no power to actually fix anything. What is true in that, and where do you think it misreads what the cross claims?
discussion.behind: Steelman the objection before answering. The aim is to grant that a suffering God does not solve the logical problem, while seeing that it answers the deeper wound of loneliness and, crucially, that the cross is not the end of the story but is followed by an empty tomb, which the objection leaves out.

discussion.q: Bonhoeffer, writing from a prison cell before the Nazis executed him, said only the suffering God can help. What do you think a man in that situation meant, and why would he find more help in a God who suffers than in a God of sheer power?
discussion.behind: Let the room sit with Bonhoeffer's context. A man facing execution finding comfort not in divine power but in divine suffering is striking. The aim is to feel that for the one actually in the pit, a God who is present in the suffering is more help than a distant God of might who might or might not intervene.

discussion.q: Bell says the cross does not explain his suffering, it tells him he does not suffer alone. Where in your own pain would it change something to know that God has been in that exact dark before you, not as a tourist but as one of the crucified?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication and application. The aim is not abstract but personal, to locate the specific pain where the companionship of a suffering God lands. Go first. Help people feel the difference between an explained suffering and a shared one, and that shared is what the cross actually offers.

objections.objection: A suffering God is a nice story, but it is just that, a story. It is emotionally consoling to imagine God hurts with us, but it does not actually change anything. The child still has cancer. A god who suffers alongside me but cannot or will not stop my suffering is a sympathetic spectator, not a savior. Sympathy is not rescue.
objections.response: Bell grants the first half completely, that a God who only suffered alongside us and did nothing else would be a consolation and not a rescue, and that sympathy without power is finally just company in the dark. So hear what the cross actually claims, because it is not merely that God feels our pain. It is that God entered our suffering in order to defeat it from the inside, that the cross is not the end of the story but the hinge of it, and that three days later the tomb was empty. The crucified God is not a sympathetic spectator who stays crucified. He is the One who took the worst that suffering and death could do, absorbed it fully, died a real death, and then walked out of the grave, which means he did not merely sit with us in the dark, he broke the dark open from the inside. The cancer is real, and Bell will not minimize it. But the claim of Easter is that death, the thing all suffering finally threatens us with, has been beaten by a God who went through it and came back, so that the companionship of the cross is backed by the power of the resurrection. Sympathy is not rescue, you are right. But this is not only sympathy. It is sympathy that ends in an empty tomb, which is next week.

objections.objection: If Jesus is God, then his suffering was not real suffering, because he knew he would rise. He knew it would be over in three days and that he would be vindicated. That is not like my suffering, where I have no guarantee, no resurrection in view, just the dark with no exit. His was a temporary inconvenience with a happy ending he could see coming.
objections.response: This is a serious objection and Bell will not brush it off, because if Christ's suffering were play-acting with a known happy ending, it would be no real solidarity at all. So look hard at the cross itself, because the Gospels go out of their way to show suffering that was anything but painless certainty. In Gethsemane, Jesus is in such agony of dread that Luke says his sweat was like great drops of blood, and he begs the Father three times to find another way, which is not the prayer of a man breezing through a temporary inconvenience. And on the cross he does not pray a confident psalm of vindication. He cries out my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, the words of a man experiencing real abandonment, real darkness, the felt absence of the Father at the worst moment. Whatever the precise theology of how the divine and human natures held in him, the Gospels insist his anguish was total and his sense of God-forsakenness was real, not performed. He did not suffer with the comfort of resurrection glowing in front of him. He suffered, as far as the cry reveals, inside the same darkness you know, the one with no felt exit. That is the point. He did not skip the dark. He went all the way into it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the specific dark you are in, and what would change if you truly believed that God had been in that exact place before you, as one of the crucified and not as a visitor?
sessions.practice: This week, take the cry of dereliction, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, and sit with it as God's own prayer in your suffering. Once, read the account of Gethsemane and the crucifixion slowly, Matthew 26 and 27, not as a familiar story but as the record of God entering the exact kind of dark you have known, the betrayal, the injustice, the abandonment. Then bring your own specific suffering to God, not asking him to explain it this time, but telling him you know he has been here, and asking him to be present in it as the One who has. Write down whether knowing God has been in the dark before you changes the dark, even without changing the circumstances, and what it is to have company there instead of an answer.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we have spent weeks asking where you are when it hurts, and tonight the answer is almost too much to take in, that you are not above the hurt, watching from a height, but inside it, on a cross, with nails through your hands and the cry of our own abandonment on your lips. We did not expect a God who bled. We expected one who explained, or one who fixed, or one who stayed serenely out of reach. Instead you climbed down into the worst of it, the betrayal, the injustice, the dark, the forsakenness, all of it, and you did not skip a single part. We do not fully understand what it means that God can suffer. But we understand that we are not alone in the pit, because you have been in it, and that changes the pit. Be present in our suffering as the One who has been here. And remind us, when we get there next, that the cross was not the end of your story. Amen.
reflection: What picture of God have I carried, a distant watcher above the suffering or a God who entered it, and how has that picture shaped whether I bring my pain to him or carry it alone?
Jesus prayed the why of forsakenness from the cross. What does it do to my own unanswered why to know it was prayed by God in human flesh, taken up into the heart of God himself?
Where would it change something, not the circumstances but the loneliness, to believe that God has been in my exact dark before me, as one of the crucified rather than as a tourist?
sessions.teaching: We have come to the center now, and everything so far has been clearing the ground for this. We stated the question at full strength and refused the cheap answers. We saw that God permits what he hates and bends it toward an end we usually cannot see, and that his answer to Job was not an explanation but his presence. And now we arrive at the thing that makes the Christian account of suffering different from every other account ever offered, the thing the skeptic Bell once was could not have predicted and could barely believe when he first understood it. Every religion and every philosophy has to do something with suffering, and almost all of them keep their god at a safe distance from it. The god of the philosophers is serene, untouched, beyond all change and therefore beyond all pain, watching the suffering of the world from a height where nothing can reach him. The various spiritualities counsel detachment, the escape from suffering by ceasing to desire. And the unbeliever, often, simply concludes that there is no one up there at all, that we suffer alone in an indifferent universe under an empty sky. And then there is the Christian claim, which the ancient world found not just false but offensive, the kind of thing no one would invent. The God who permits suffering did not stay outside it. He climbed down into it. He took on a body that could be beaten and a heart that could be broken, and he entered the suffering of the world from the inside, all the way to the bottom of it, to a Roman cross, the most agonizing and humiliating death the ancient world had devised. Now I have to be honest about what this does and does not do, because if I oversell it I will lose the skeptic, and the skeptic is who I am writing toward. A suffering God does not, by itself, solve the logical problem of evil. If you came tonight for a tighter argument, a crucified God is not it, and I grant that fully. But here is what I have come to believe, and it took me years. The logical problem was never the deepest part of the wound. Underneath the argument, in every person I have ever sat with in real suffering, the deepest part is not a syllogism. It is the loneliness. It is the terrible sense that you are suffering alone, in the dark, under the gaze of a God who, if he exists at all, is watching from a comfortable height and feeling nothing. That is the part that breaks people. Not the philosophy. The aloneness. And it is exactly that wound that the cross goes to the center of. Look at what God actually entered. Not a symbolic, sanitized suffering, but the real thing, in all its specific horror. He was betrayed by a friend, sold for the price of a slave, abandoned by the people closest to him when he needed them most, condemned by a justice system that knew he was innocent, tortured, mocked, and nailed through the hands and feet to a piece of wood, left to die slowly in front of his mother. And then, at the very end, he prayed something I want you to hear with the full weight of these last weeks on it. He cried out, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me. Do you hear what that is. That is the question. That is the why of session one, the cry of the abandoned, the how long and the where are you of the Psalms, and it is being prayed, here, at the bottom of everything, by God in human flesh. The question this whole study has been circling, the one we worried might be a failure of faith to even ask, turns out to have been prayed by the Son of God himself, in the darkest hour there has ever been. Which means that when you ask it, you are not standing outside the faith shaking your fist at it. You are standing in the deepest company there is. The question has been taken up into the very heart of God. Now the skeptic has a sharp reply ready, and I respect it, so let me state it at full strength. A suffering God, the skeptic says, is just a sad story we tell ourselves so we do not feel alone. It is consoling, sure, but it does not change anything. The child still has cancer. A god who suffers alongside me but does not stop my suffering is a sympathetic spectator, not a savior, and sympathy is not rescue. I grant the second half of that entirely. A God who only suffered with us and did nothing else would be company in the dark and nothing more, and company is not the same as rescue. But hear what the cross actually claims, because it is not merely that God feels our pain from beside us. It is that God entered the suffering in order to defeat it from the inside, that the cross is not a freestanding sad story but the hinge of a longer one, and that the One who went into the grave did not stay there. We will get to the empty tomb next week, because without it the cross is only the most beautiful tragedy ever told. But hold this much tonight. The crucified God is not a spectator who stays crucified. He is the One who took the full weight of suffering and death onto himself and broke it open from the other side. There is a second objection, just as serious, so I will not dodge it. If Jesus is God, the objection runs, then his suffering was not really like mine, because he knew he would rise. He had the happy ending in view the whole time, while my suffering has no guarantee, just the dark with no visible exit. This deserves a careful answer, because if Christ's suffering were play-acting with a known happy ending glowing in front of him, it would be no real solidarity at all. So look hard at the Gospels, which go out of their way to show the opposite. In Gethsemane, the night before he died, Jesus is in such agony of dread that Luke, a physician, says his sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground, and he falls on his face and begs the Father three times to find another way. That is not the prayer of a man strolling confidently toward a sure reward. And on the cross he does not pray a serene psalm of certain vindication. He cries the cry of dereliction, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, the words of a man in real abandonment, the felt absence of the Father at the worst possible moment. Whatever the deep theology of how the divine and human held together in him, and the church has handled that mystery with care for twenty centuries, the Gospels insist his anguish was total and his God-forsakenness was not performed but real. As far as that cry reveals, he suffered inside the same darkness you know, the one with no felt exit. He did not skip the dark. He went all the way into it. And this brings me to the man I most want you to meet tonight, because he understood this from inside a place very few of us will ever be. Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a German pastor and theologian who refused to bless Hitler's regime, was arrested, and was imprisoned by the Nazis, and eventually hanged at a concentration camp in April of 1945, weeks before the war ended. From his prison cell, in letters that were later collected and published as Letters and Papers from Prison, he wrote some of the most searching things ever written about God and suffering, and he wrote them not as a comfortable theologian theorizing but as a man who knew he would likely be killed. And Bonhoeffer wrote, against everything our instincts expect, that only the suffering God can help. He had come to see that the God the Bible points us to is not first of all the God of power in the world, the strong arm we keep begging to intervene and fix things, but the God who is with us precisely by being weak and suffering alongside us, the powerless and suffering God who alone, he said, can be beside us in our own suffering. Think about who is saying that, and from where. A man in a Nazi prison, facing execution, with every reason to want a God of overwhelming power to break him out, and what he found that actually helped, what he could lean his whole weight on as the dark closed in, was not a God of might but a God who suffers, a God who was, in that very cell, beside him because he had been in cells and on crosses himself. That is the testimony not of an armchair but of a death row, and it is worth more than a thousand tidy theodicies. So here is the verdict, the center of everything. The cross does not explain your suffering. I told you in the first session I would not hand you an explanation, and I am keeping that promise, even here, even at the center. The cross does something the explanation never could. It tells you that whatever pit you are in, however dark, however lonely, God has been there before you, and not as a tourist who visited and left, but as one of the crucified, who knew the betrayal and the injustice and the physical agony and even the forsakenness, the felt absence of God in the worst hour, all of it. You do not suffer alone. The sky is not empty and the One above it is not untouched. He came down. He is in the pit with you, because he has been in the pit himself. And that companionship, the skeptic is right, would still not be enough if it ended there, if it were only sympathy with no power behind it. But it does not end there, and that is where we are going next, to the morning that the dark of the cross did not get the last word, to the empty tomb, where the God who entered death walked back out of it, and where suffering meets not an explanation but a defeat.

scriptureStudy.note: A man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows. The prophetic portrait of a Messiah who does not stand above suffering but takes it into himself, fulfilled at the cross.
My God, my God, why have you forsaken me. Jesus prays the cry of dereliction, the very question of the suffering soul, taking the why of the abandoned up into the experience of God in human flesh.

Being in agony he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground. The Gospels insist Christ's suffering was real anguish and dread, not painless certainty, which makes his solidarity with sufferers genuine.

We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are. The God we approach is not distant from human suffering but has entered it fully, which is the ground of drawing near to him in pain.

Because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted. Christ's own suffering is named as the very thing that qualifies him to help the suffering, presence translated into aid.

Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. The God who was under no obligation to suffer chose to enter the lowest place, the descent that grounds the whole claim of a crucified God.
Jesus wept. At the grave of his friend, knowing he would raise him, God in the flesh still weeps with the grieving, refusing to stand above human sorrow even when he holds the power to undo it.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the doctrine of divine impassibility and the long argument over whether and how God suffers, because this session presses on one of the deepest questions in Christian theology and a serious group should know it is contested ground handled by faithful believers on both sides. The classical tradition, drawing on the church fathers, has often affirmed that God in his divine nature is impassible, not subject to suffering or being acted upon from outside, in order to protect that God is not a victim swept along by forces greater than himself. On this reading the suffering of Christ is real but is borne in his human nature, the eternal Son experiencing human suffering through the incarnation without the divine nature being diminished. A powerful modern stream, writing in the shadow of the atrocities of the twentieth century, has pressed instead the suffering of God, arguing that the cross reveals a God who genuinely takes pain into his own life, and the German theologian Jürgen Moltmann gave this its most influential statement in his work on the crucified God. A serious group should state both with care and recognize that the creeds bind us to the genuine deity and genuine humanity of Christ and to the reality of the cross, while leaving the precise metaphysics of divine suffering more open than either camp sometimes admits. The study lands on the pastoral center both sides share, that in Christ God truly entered human suffering, that the incarnation means there is now no human pit God has not known from the inside, and it sets beside this Bonhoeffer's hard-won conviction, written from a Nazi prison in his Letters and Papers from Prison, that only the suffering God can help. The discipline is to confess the reality without resolving the mystery, and to leave the deeper metaphysics held with the humility the subject demands.

memoryVerse.text: Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted.

sessions.title: Hope That Does Not Disappoint
sessions.aim: To end the study where the Christian hope actually lands, not in an explanation of suffering but in its final defeat, the resurrection of Christ and the new creation where every tear is wiped away, so that suffering is neither minimized nor rationalized but named as real and then named as not the last word.
sessions.summary: We have refused, for five weeks, to explain suffering away, and we are not going to start now. The Christian hope is not that suffering was secretly fine, or that it all made sense in the end, or that you will understand it one day. The Christian hope is stranger and stronger than understanding. It is that suffering, real and terrible and unexplained, is going to be defeated. The first question is what makes that more than wishful thinking, because every grieving person has been told to hope, and hope can sound like a sedative handed to people with no reason for it. Bell takes the strong form of the suspicion, that the promise of heaven is the oldest trick in the book, pie in the sky to keep the suffering quiet, an opiate that asks people to endure injustice now for a reward later that conveniently cannot be checked. He grants how it has been misused exactly that way. But Christian hope is not a vague optimism or an unverifiable promise. It is grounded in an event, the resurrection of Jesus, the morning the cross did not get the last word, the God who entered death walking back out of it, the first piece of the new creation breaking into the old. Paul says our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed, and he does not say it from a comfortable study but as a man beaten, imprisoned, and finally killed for his faith. The whole creation, he says, groans like a woman in labor, and labor pains are real agony that is nonetheless producing something. The turn, and the end of the whole study, is Revelation's vision, God himself dwelling with his people, and he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying nor pain anymore. Not suffering explained. Suffering ended, wiped from every face by the hand of God. The study does not close with a resolution of the problem of evil. It closes with the only thing that was ever big enough to answer it, a hope grounded in an empty tomb, and a promise that the dark, which is real, is not the end of the story.

keyScripture.why: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away, the Bible's final word on suffering, which is not an explanation but a defeat, every tear wiped from every face by the hand of God himself, the dark named as real and then named as not the last word.

discussion.q: The Christian hope is not that suffering made sense but that it will be defeated. What is the difference between those two, between an explained suffering and a defeated one, and which do you find you have actually been longing for?
discussion.behind: Open by distinguishing the two hopes. We often think we want the explanation, but the deeper longing is usually for the suffering to be ended and undone. The aim is to feel that the gospel offers the second, not the first, and that defeat is a larger hope than understanding.

discussion.q: The skeptic says heaven is pie in the sky, an opiate to keep the suffering quiet, a reward that conveniently cannot be checked. Where has that critique been earned by the church, and where does it misread what Christian hope actually rests on?
discussion.behind: Steelman the objection honestly. The church has used heaven to pacify the oppressed, and that abuse is real. The aim is to grant it while seeing that genuine Christian hope is grounded in a claimed event, the resurrection, not an unverifiable promise, and that it has historically fueled justice rather than only sedating it.

discussion.q: Paul says our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed, and he says it as a man who was beaten, imprisoned, and killed for his faith. Does it change the line to know who said it and from where?
discussion.behind: Ground the hope in the credibility of the witness. The line sounds glib from a comfortable person and weighty from a sufferer. The aim is to feel that Paul is not minimizing suffering from a distance but weighing it from inside, having suffered enormously, which makes his verdict a tested one rather than a cheap one.

discussion.q: Revelation says God himself will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Sit with that image, God's own hand on your face. What does it offer that a mere end to suffering, or an explanation of it, would not?
discussion.behind: Let the room dwell in the specific tenderness of the image. It is not just that suffering ends but that God personally attends to each griever. The aim is to feel the intimacy of it, that the final answer to suffering is not a cosmic mechanism but the hand of a Father on a wet face, presence and defeat together.

discussion.q: Bell ends not by resolving the problem of evil but by pointing to an empty tomb and a promise. After five weeks, where do you land, and what will you carry out of this study into your own unanswered suffering?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study without forcing resolution. The aim is honest integration, not a tidy bow. Let people name where they actually are, doubt included, and what they are taking with them. Go first. End on weight and hope held together, with no pressure to have arrived anywhere in particular.

objections.objection: Heaven is the oldest trick in the book. Promise the suffering a reward they cannot verify, after they are dead, so they will endure their misery quietly instead of demanding justice now. It is an opiate. The powerful have always loved a religion that tells the suffering to wait for the next life, and I am not falling for it.
objections.response: Bell grants that this critique has been earned, again and again, that the promise of heaven has been used exactly as an opiate, to tell slaves to obey their masters and the oppressed to wait quietly for a reward, and that any honest Christian has to own that abuse rather than dodge it. So hear two things the critique misses. First, the resurrection hope is not an unverifiable promise floated to pacify people, it rests on a claimed event in history, the empty tomb, which the first Christians died insisting they had witnessed, and you can investigate that claim rather than dismiss it as wishful thinking. Second, and against the opiate charge directly, the hope of resurrection has historically fueled the fight against injustice at least as often as it has sedated it, because people who believe the suffering will be defeated and the wrongs finally judged are freed to confront evil now without despair, knowing their resistance is not futile. The same hope that comforts the dying has put reformers and martyrs in front of tyrants. A hope that the dark is not the last word does not have to mean accepting the dark, it can mean fighting it with the confidence that you are on the winning side of history. The opiate reading is a real abuse of the hope, not the hope itself.

objections.objection: Even if there is a new creation where every tear is wiped away, that does not undo the suffering that already happened. The child who died in agony still died in agony. A future where it stops does not reach back and unmake the past horror. Wiping away the tears later does not change the fact that the tears were shed.
objections.response: This is the deepest objection of all, and Bell will not pretend the future simply erases the past, because the cross itself refuses that. The risen Christ still bears the scars, the wounds are not deleted, they are healed and glorified but still there, which suggests the new creation does not pretend the suffering never happened. So the Christian hope is not amnesia, not a future that acts as if the past horror was nothing. It is something the New Testament gestures at but does not fully spell out, a redemption deep enough to reach backward, where the very wounds become, somehow, the site of glory rather than only of loss, the way Christ's scars are now the proof of his love rather than only the marks of his torture. Bell will be honest that he cannot fully explain how a future good reaches back to redeem a past agony, and that anyone who claims to have that mechanism mapped is overreaching. This is the strongest objection he has not fully answered, and he names it as such. But he holds up the scarred and risen Christ as the hint, the One whose worst day became the hinge of salvation, as the ground for trusting that in the new creation the tears that were shed will not merely be stopped but somehow gathered up and answered, by a God who does not forget them and does not waste them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you truly believed that the suffering you carry will one day be not explained but defeated, and that God himself will wipe the tears from your face, what would you dare to hope for that you have stopped letting yourself hope for?
sessions.practice: This week, hold the two halves of the Christian hope together on purpose, and do not skip either. First, do not minimize your suffering, name it as real, let it be as heavy as it is, refusing to spiritualize it into something smaller. Then, deliberately, read Revelation 21 and Romans 8:18 through 25 slowly, and let yourself imagine the promise concretely, not suffering explained but suffering ended, God's own hand wiping the tears from your face, the specific grief you carry undone. Sit in the tension of a real present grief and a real future hope without collapsing one into the other. If you have stopped hoping because hope kept disappointing you, bring even that to God. Write down what it is to grieve and to hope at the same time, and whether the empty tomb gives you any ground to stand on that wishful thinking would not.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we have asked for five weeks where you are when it hurts, and we have not been given a tidy answer, and we have stopped needing one as badly as we thought we did, because we have found something better than an explanation. We have found that you permit what you hate and bend it past its makers. We have found that you answer the sufferer with your presence. We have found that you did not stay above the pain but climbed into it on a cross. And now we find that the cross was not the end, that the tomb is empty, that the dark you entered you also defeated. We grieve still, and you do not ask us to stop, because the tears are real and you do not pretend otherwise. But you have promised to wipe them away, every one, with your own hand, and to make an end of death and mourning and crying and pain. We will carry that out of this room. Not suffering explained. Suffering defeated. And until that morning, your presence in the dark, which has turned out to be enough. Amen.
reflection: Have I been longing for my suffering to be explained when the deeper hope on offer is for it to be defeated, and what changes if I let myself want the larger thing?
Where has the promise of future hope been used to silence me, or to silence others, and how is the resurrection hope different from the opiate the skeptic rightly rejects?
If God himself will one day wipe the tears from my face, how does that promise, grounded in an empty tomb rather than wishful thinking, change the way I carry an unhealed grief now?
sessions.teaching: We have spent five weeks refusing to explain suffering away, and I am not going to break that promise in the final session, even though this is where you might expect the resolution to finally arrive. There is no resolution coming, not the kind you wanted in week one, the airtight account that makes the suffering make sense. The Christian hope is not that suffering was secretly fine, or that it all clicked into place in the end, or even that you will one day understand the reason for it. The Christian hope is stranger than understanding, and stronger. It is that suffering, real and terrible and unexplained, is going to be defeated. An explanation would tell you why the child died. A defeat undoes the death. We keep asking God for the explanation, the small thing, when what he has actually promised is the enormous thing, not that suffering will be justified but that it will be destroyed. Now the moment I say hope, a sharp and fair suspicion should rise, and I want to take it at its full strength, because it is the skeptic's strongest card and the church has handed it to him over and over. The suspicion is that heaven is the oldest trick in the book. Promise the suffering a reward, after they are safely dead, where it conveniently cannot be checked, so that they will endure their misery quietly now instead of demanding justice. It is, in the famous phrase, an opiate, and the powerful have always loved a religion that keeps the suffering docile. I am not going to dodge this, because it is true, it has been used exactly that way. Slaveholders preached heaven to slaves to keep them obedient. That is a real abuse, and any honest Christian has to own it. But hear what the abuse misses. Christian hope is not a vague optimism floated to pacify people. It is grounded in a claimed event, in a specific place, on a specific morning. The tomb was empty. The God who entered death on Friday walked back out of it on Sunday, and the first Christians did not preach a comforting idea, they preached a thing they insisted they had seen, and they died, most of them violently, insisting on it. You can investigate that claim, and it is a very different thing from wishful thinking, because wishful thinking does not get you executed for refusing to recant. And against the opiate charge directly, the belief that suffering will be defeated and every injustice finally judged has, at least as often as it has sedated people, set them on fire to fight injustice now, because if you believe the dark is not the last word, you are freed to confront it without despair. The same hope that comforts the dying has marched reformers and martyrs straight at tyrants. A hope that the dark will be defeated does not have to mean accepting the dark. It can mean fighting it with confidence. So this is not pie in the sky. Now let me put the right witness in front of you, because who says a thing about suffering matters as much as what is said, and we learned that with Bonhoeffer last week. The Apostle Paul writes, in his letter to the Romans, that he considers the sufferings of this present time not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us. Read flat, that line sounds glib, the kind of thing a comfortable person says to a hurting one. But consider who wrote it. Paul lists, elsewhere, what his life of faith had cost him. Beaten with rods, whipped, stoned and left for dead, shipwrecked, imprisoned repeatedly, and finally, by reliable tradition, executed for his faith in Rome. This is not a man weighing suffering from a distance and waving it off. This is a man who suffered as much as almost anyone in this room ever will, weighing his own real agony against what he believed was coming, and saying, having felt the full weight of both, that the suffering does not tip the scale against the glory. That is not a glib line. That is a tested verdict, rendered by a man who had every right to render it. And Paul gives the broken world an image that honors the suffering even while it points past it. The whole creation, he says, has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. Labor pains are real, severe agony, and Paul does not pretend otherwise. But they are agony that is producing something, the pains not of death but of birth, the labor of a creation straining toward its rebirth. The suffering is real. It is also not pointless thrashing in the dark. It is labor, and there is a child coming. So where does this study land, after five weeks. It lands in the last pages of the Bible, in a vision John was given of the end, and I am going to read it to you, because nothing I could say improves on it. Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away. Notice what that is, and what it is not. It is not suffering explained. There is no paragraph in Revelation that finally tells us why, no answer to Ivan that closes the case. John is not given the explanation, and neither are we. What he is given is suffering defeated. Death, the thing all suffering finally threatens us with, is abolished. Mourning and crying and pain, gone, not rationalized, not justified, but ended. And notice the tenderness of how it ends, because this is the thing that undoes me every time. God himself will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Not by some impersonal cosmic mechanism. God himself, with his own hand, will reach out and wipe the tears from your face, one griever at a time, the way a father wipes the face of a child who has cried himself out. The final answer to all the suffering of the world turns out not to be an argument at all, it never was, all the way back to Job. It is a Person, and a hand, and a face, and the end of every tear. Now I owe you one last honesty, because there is a deep objection even to this, and I will not end on a false note. Someone is thinking, even a future where the tears are wiped away does not undo the tears that were already shed. The child still died in agony. A future that stops the suffering does not reach back and unmake the past horror. That is the strongest objection I have, and I am going to tell you plainly that I cannot fully answer it. But I can hand you the one hint Scripture gives, and it is a strange and powerful one. When Jesus rose from the dead, he still had the wounds. He shows Thomas the scars in his hands and his side. The wounds were not deleted, as if the suffering had never happened. They were healed, and glorified, and yet still there, and they had become the very proof of his love rather than only the marks of his torture. Which suggests that the new creation is not amnesia, not a future that pretends the past horror was nothing. It suggests a redemption somehow deep enough to reach backward, where the very places we were broken become, in a way I cannot map and will not pretend to, the places where the love and the victory show most clearly. Anyone who claims to have that fully mapped is overreaching, and I would rather leave you with an honest mystery than a dishonest closure. But I can point you to the scarred and risen Christ, whose worst day became the hinge of the salvation of the world, as the ground for trusting that the tears already shed are not lost, not forgotten, not wasted, but held by a God who will not only stop our crying but somehow answer it. So we end where we began, with the question still standing, and yet everything changed. I told you in the first session I would not hand you an explanation, and I have kept that promise through five weeks, because the Bible never gives the explanation and I will not invent what God withheld. What it gives instead is this. A God who permits what he hates and bends it past its makers. A God who answers the sufferer with his presence. A God who did not stay above the pain but climbed all the way down into it, onto a cross, into the cry of forsakenness itself. And a God who did not stay in the grave, who walked out of it on the third day as the first light of a new creation, and who has promised that one day he will wipe every tear from every face with his own hand, and make an end of death forever. That is not the problem of evil solved. It is the problem of evil outlasted, and answered not with a reason but with a Person, and a promise, and an empty tomb. The dark is real. I have not pretended otherwise for one minute of this study, and I will not start now. But the dark is not the last word. The last word is a morning, and a hand on a wet face, and the One who has been in the dark himself saying, behold, I am making all things new. Carry that out of this room. And if tonight the grief is still heavier than the hope, that is honest, and you are not behind. Bring the grief and the hope both, and keep coming, because the One who entered the dark is the One who will end it, and he has not lost track of a single tear.

scriptureStudy.note: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying nor pain anymore. The Bible's final word on suffering is not an explanation but a defeat, every tear wiped away by the hand of God himself.

I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us. Paul, a man who suffered enormously and was killed for his faith, weighs real agony against coming glory and renders a tested verdict, not a glib one.

The whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. The suffering of the world is real agony, but it is the agony of labor, severe pain that is nonetheless producing the birth of a new creation, not meaningless thrashing.

Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your victory. O death, where is your sting. The resurrection turns the great enemy into a defeated foe, the ground of the hope that suffering and death are not the final reality.

Put your finger here, and see my hands. The risen Christ still bears the scars, the wounds healed and glorified but not erased, the hint that the new creation redeems rather than forgets the suffering of the old.

He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord God will wipe away tears from all faces. The promise Revelation echoes is rooted deep in the prophets, the ancient hope that God himself would personally end death and grief.

Born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. Christian hope is named as living and grounded specifically in the resurrection, an event, not a vague optimism or an unverifiable promise.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the relation between Christian hope and the charge that religion is an opiate, because the critique is serious, was made seriously, and deserves a serious answer rather than a dismissal. The charge in its sharpest modern form holds that the promise of a future reward functions to pacify the suffering and the oppressed, draining the energy that might otherwise go toward changing their conditions now, and a serious group should grant without flinching that the church has often deserved the charge, preaching a heaven that told the enslaved and the exploited to endure quietly. But the historical record is more double-edged than the critique allows. The same resurrection hope has repeatedly fueled rather than dampened the confrontation with injustice, because a people convinced that evil will finally be judged and that their resistance is not futile have been freed to oppose tyranny without the paralysis of despair, and movements for the abolition of slavery and for civil rights drew deeply on the conviction that the moral arc of the universe bends toward a justice God himself guarantees. Set this beside the New Testament's own refusal to make hope a substitute for action, the insistence that those who hope for the new creation are precisely the ones called to embody its justice now, and the charge begins to look like an indictment of a distortion rather than of the thing itself. A serious group should also weigh the difference between hope grounded in an event and hope grounded in mere wish, between the resurrection as a claimed historical occurrence open to investigation and a generic optimism that asks nothing and verifies nothing. The discipline of this final session is to hold the hope honestly, neither as an opiate that excuses passivity before evil nor as a wishful sedative immune to evidence, but as a tested conviction, grounded in an empty tomb, that the suffering which is real and which the study has refused for five weeks to minimize is nonetheless not the last word, and that the God who entered the dark has promised to end it.

leaderPrimer: Plan every session as if the wound in the room were fresh, because somewhere at your table it is. A diagnosis that came this year, a child who is not okay, a grave with new grass on it, and for that person the doctrine of providence is not a topic. It is the question they cry into a pillow. Every sentence you say about the sovereignty of God will land on their particular catastrophe, so weigh each one before it leaves your mouth. The hazard of this study has a name, and the name is Job's friends. They were orthodox. Most of their sentences would pass a doctrine exam. They took the true idea that God governs all things and used it to explain a specific man's specific agony, and at the end of the book God's anger falls on them for not speaking rightly of him, not on the sufferer who had shouted his complaint at heaven (Job 42:7). You will feel their temptation weekly, because tidy sovereignty is easier to say than the honest thing, which is that God permits what he hates for reasons we mostly cannot see from inside the permitting. Say the honest thing. Never explain anyone's tragedy to them. Never connect their loss to a lesson, a purpose they should be seeing, a hidden good you have identified on their behalf. That arithmetic belongs to God alone, and every human who attempts it wounds. What you can do is keep the room moving toward the only answer Scripture finally gives, which is not an argument but a Person with scars. Bell hit the problem of evil as an atheist and stayed outside the faith for years because of it, and since becoming a pastor he has prayed beside hospital beds for healing that did not come. He does not resolve the question in five weeks, and neither will you, and saying so plainly in session one will win you more trust than any theodicy. Expect anger at God to surface, and when it does, do not defend him. He has never asked for that, and the psalms he inspired contain more complaint than your group has yet dared (Psalm 13). Your posture to the end is the one the friends abandoned, quiet, near, unshocked. Sit closer than you explain. That is the whole assignment.

faq.q: Is this study going to give me an answer to why God allows suffering?
faq.a: No, and it is honest about that from the first session. There is no tidy answer to the problem of evil, no paragraph that makes the suffering make sense, and the study refuses to pretend otherwise because the studies that pretend are the ones that wound. What it does instead is take the question at its full strength, refuse the cheap answers that survive only by quietly dropping one of the three claims, that God is good, that God is able, that evil is real, and walk toward the only response Scripture finally gives, which is not an argument but a Person who entered the suffering himself. If you come looking for the explanation that closes the case, you will not find it here, because the Bible does not give it. What you will find is a God who permits what he hates and bends it past its makers, who answers the sufferer with his presence, who climbed into the pain on a cross, and who has promised to defeat suffering rather than merely justify it.

faq.q: How is this different from the grief study or the lament study?
faq.a: They sit next to each other but they are not the same. The grief study walks through personal loss, the death of someone you love, and how to carry it. The lament study teaches the prayer language of sorrow, how to bring grief honestly to God in the words Scripture gives. This study is the harder intellectual and pastoral question underneath both, the problem of evil itself, why a good and sovereign God permits suffering at all. It is theodicy and providence, written toward the skeptic first, the person whose faith broke or never formed over the suffering of the innocent. If you are carrying a specific fresh loss, the grief and lament studies may meet you more directly, and this one can wait. If the question that haunts you is the larger why, whether a good God can be squared with a world like this, this is the study built for that.

faq.q: I am a skeptic, and the problem of evil is exactly why I cannot believe. Will this study take that seriously or just try to talk me out of it?
faq.a: It is written toward you first, and it takes your objection more seriously than most believers do. The first session states the problem at its full strength, in the form the honest atheist gives it, including Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov, who does not deny God but refuses a paradise bought with the unavenged tears of a tortured child, and it grants that the objection is genuinely strong, not a puzzle for clever people to swat away. The writer came to God from atheism, and the problem of evil was the wall he could not climb for years, so he is not handling your question from the outside. The study will not pretend the logical difficulty disappears, and it will not hand you a proof. What it offers is a claim worth weighing, that the dilemma is not as airtight as it looks, and a response that is not an argument but a God who entered the suffering himself and walked back out of the grave. You can finish still disbelieving and be met honestly.

faq.q: Does the study claim that everything happens for a reason?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to take that phrase apart, because it has wounded more grieving people than almost any other. Session two draws the line carefully. Scripture says God works good out of evil, in Joseph's words, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, and in Paul's, that God works in all things toward good. It does not say all things are good, or that the evil was secretly a blessing, or that every horror has a visible purpose you should be able to find. Joseph names the evil as real evil even while trusting God worked good through it, and he says it from the throne, years later, in hindsight he did not have in the pit. The study insists we are usually in the pit, not the throne, that we often cannot read God's purpose at all, and that demanding a sufferer produce a tidy reason in the moment is cruelty dressed as faith. It refuses to call evil good, ever.

faq.q: Why does the book of Job get a whole session when God never even answers Job's question?
faq.a: Because that is precisely the point, and it is one of the most important things the Bible says about suffering. Job is the Scripture's whole book on the problem of evil, and the most significant thing about it is what it refuses to do, which is explain. Job is blameless, God says so, and he suffers terribly for reasons he is never told. When God finally answers, he does not give a reason, he gives his presence and a flood of questions that put Job back inside a creation too large for his own accounting. And crucially, God is angry at the end, not at Job who protested and shook his fist, but at the friends who defended God with tidy theology, the formula that suffering must be punishment for sin. The protester is vindicated, the explainers are rebuked. Session three sits in that, because it frees us from the friends' lie and teaches the strange truth that God's deepest answer to suffering is not an argument but an encounter, presence over explanation.

faq.q: What does it mean that God suffers? Does not God being God mean he is above all that?
faq.a: This is a genuinely deep and contested question, and session four handles it with care rather than pretending it is simple. The classical tradition has often held that God in his divine nature does not suffer, in order to protect that he is not a victim swept along by forces greater than himself, and that the suffering of Christ is real but borne in his human nature through the incarnation. A powerful modern stream, written in the shadow of the twentieth century's atrocities, has pressed that the cross reveals a God who genuinely takes pain into his own life. The study states both and lands on the pastoral center they share, that in Christ God truly entered human suffering, that there is now no human pit God has not known from the inside. It holds the reality, that the cross is God's own entry into our pain, without claiming to have mapped the deeper metaphysics, which Scripture itself does not fully spell out.

faq.q: Who was Bonhoeffer, and why does the study lean on him?
faq.a: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a German pastor and theologian who refused to support Hitler's regime, was imprisoned by the Nazis, and was executed at a concentration camp in April of 1945, weeks before the war ended. From his prison cell he wrote letters later collected as Letters and Papers from Prison, and in them he wrote that only the suffering God can help, that the help we need comes not from a God of sheer power in the world but from the God who is weak and suffering alongside us. The study leans on him because of who he was and where he wrote from. A man facing execution, with every reason to want a God of overwhelming power to break him out, found that what he could actually lean his weight on was a God who suffers, a God who had been in cells and on crosses himself. That is the testimony of a death row, not an armchair, and it is worth more than a thousand tidy arguments about suffering.

faq.q: If God just wipes away the tears later, does that really fix the suffering that already happened?
faq.a: This is the deepest objection in the study, and session five names it as the strongest one the writer cannot fully answer rather than dodging it. A future where suffering stops does not, on its face, reach back and unmake the past horror, the child who died in agony still died in agony. The one hint Scripture gives is strange and powerful. When Jesus rose, he still bore the scars, the wounds healed and glorified but not erased, which suggests the new creation is not amnesia, not a future that pretends the past was nothing, but a redemption somehow deep enough to reach backward, where the very wounds become the site of glory rather than only of loss. The study is honest that it cannot map how a future good redeems a past agony, and that anyone claiming to have it mapped is overreaching. It points to the scarred and risen Christ as the ground for trusting that the tears already shed are not lost or wasted, but held by a God who will answer them.

faq.q: Is the hope of heaven just a way to keep suffering people quiet?
faq.a: The study grants that this critique has been earned, that the promise of heaven has been used as an opiate, telling the enslaved and the oppressed to endure quietly and wait for a reward, and that any honest Christian has to own that abuse. But it points to two things the critique misses. First, the resurrection hope is not an unverifiable promise floated to pacify people, it rests on a claimed event in history, the empty tomb, which the first Christians died insisting they had witnessed, and which you can investigate rather than dismiss. Second, against the opiate charge directly, the same hope has historically fueled the fight against injustice at least as often as it has sedated it, because people who believe evil will finally be judged and their resistance is not futile are freed to confront it now without despair. A hope that the dark is not the last word does not require accepting the dark. It can mean fighting it with confidence.

faq.q: I am in fresh grief right now. Is this study going to make it worse?
faq.a: It might be too soon, and that is worth saying plainly. This study is built to take the intellectual question seriously, and if you are in the raw early weeks of a loss, the grief study or the lament study may meet you more gently and directly than this one. That said, the study is written by someone who has buried people he loved, and it refuses at every turn to explain suffering away or to hand you a formula, which is often what makes fresh grief worse. It validates the feeling and never the despair. It protects the grieving from the room's instinct to explain their pain. And it keeps a path to real help visible, because suffering can press past what a study can hold. If you are in acute distress, please do not carry it alone, tell your group leader, a pastor, or a counselor, and if you are in danger, reach out to a crisis line and stay with someone safe. The study can wait. You matter more than finishing it.

faq.q: Why does the study keep refusing to give a clean answer? Is not that just dodging the hard question?
faq.a: It is the opposite of dodging, it is refusing to lie. The clean answer to the problem of evil does not exist, and the studies that hand one out are not braver, they are less honest, and the suffering can feel the dishonesty. The Bible itself withholds the explanation. Job demands one and never gets it. Jesus prays the why from the cross. What Scripture gives instead of an explanation is harder and more durable, a God who permits what he hates and bends it toward an end, who answers the sufferer with his presence, who entered the pain on a cross, and who has promised to defeat suffering rather than justify it. The study refuses the clean answer because keeping that promise to the suffering, that no one will hand them a paragraph too small for their wound, is the whole point. A faith honest enough to keep its own unanswered questions in the room is more trustworthy, especially to the skeptic, than one that pretends to have closed the case.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I do not have the problem of evil figured out myself?
faq.a: Your unresolved question is not a disqualification, it may be your best qualification, because no one has the problem of evil figured out and the moment you posture as though you do, you lose the room. The study is built to be led by a fellow sufferer, not by an expert who dispenses answers, and every discussion question carries the thinking behind it, every objection is steelmanned for you, and every session ends in prayer rather than a tidy resolution, so you are not improvising. Your honesty about your own unanswered suffering, the loss you cannot account for, the prayer that went unanswered, may be the most freeing thing in the room, the permission that lets others stop performing certainty. What you do need is to take the skeptic's question seriously, refuse to let the group explain away real pain, protect the grieving, keep a path to real help visible, and point everyone, yourself first, to the God who entered the dark and walked back out of it. Read the leader primer, be honest with God and the group about where you actually are, and trust the material.

timeline.event: In the patriarchal narratives Joseph is sold into slavery by his brothers and raised to save them, later naming the two intentions in one event, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, the clearest scriptural statement of providence and the spine of the study's second session.

The book of Job is composed, the Bible's whole treatment of the problem of evil, in which a blameless man suffers without explanation, his friends' formula that suffering is punishment for sin is rebuked, and God answers not with a reason but with his presence out of the whirlwind.

The psalmists give Israel the language of honest complaint, how long O Lord, my God my God why have you forsaken me, prayers that bring the question of God's apparent absence in suffering directly to God without rebuke, modeling that the cry is permitted.

The philosopher Epicurus frames an early sharp form of the problem of evil, the dilemma of a God either unwilling or unable to prevent evil, preserved through later writers, marking how old and serious the question is rather than a modern complaint.

Jesus is betrayed, condemned in a rigged trial, and crucified, praying from the cross the cry of dereliction, my God my God why have you forsaken me, God in human flesh entering the worst of human suffering, and three days later the tomb is found empty.

Paul writes to the Romans that the present sufferings are not worth comparing with the coming glory, that creation groans in the pains of childbirth, and that God works in all things toward good, weighing real agony as a man who would himself be martyred for the faith.

John records the vision of Revelation, the new creation where God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear from their eyes, where death and mourning and crying and pain are no more, the Bible's final word on suffering as defeat rather than explanation.

Augustine develops his account of evil as the privation of good, a corruption of what God made good rather than a thing in itself, shaping how the Western church would think about the nature of evil for over a thousand years.

Fyodor Dostoevsky publishes The Brothers Karamazov, in which the character Ivan voices the problem of evil at its most honest and devastating, refusing a final harmony purchased by the unavenged suffering of a tortured child and respectfully returning his ticket, the form the study uses to state the objection at full strength.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a German pastor imprisoned for resisting Hitler, is executed at a concentration camp weeks before the war ends, having written from his cell, in letters later published as Letters and Papers from Prison, that only the suffering God can help, the witness at the center of the study's fourth session.

C. S. Lewis publishes nothing on this in this year, but his earlier The Problem of Pain (1940) and later A Grief Observed (1961) frame the question both as an argument and as a wound, the second written from inside his own bereavement, refusing the tidy answers he had once offered.

The philosopher Alvin Plantinga publishes the mature form of his free will defense, widely held to show that there is no strict logical contradiction in an all-good, all-powerful God permitting evil for a sufficient reason, shifting the modern debate from the logical to the evidential and existential form of the problem.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here, and thank you for the courage it took, because this is the hardest question there is and most of us have been told to keep quiet about it. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can say I do not understand how a good God allows this here. You can say I lost my faith over this, or I am barely holding it, or I am still angry at God about something that happened. Nobody is going to grade your faith or hand you a formula to fix your grief. Second, this study is not going to give you a tidy answer to why God allows suffering, because there is not one, and anybody who hands you one is not being honest with you. What we are after is something harder and sturdier than an answer. Third, the writer puts himself inside all of this, and so will I. He came to God from atheism, and this exact question was the wall he could not get over for years. I have my own unanswered suffering too, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. We are not solving a puzzle from above. We are walking toward something together. Tonight we are sitting with this part of the question: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what Scripture says here. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the actual suffering we carry or watch others carry, because that is where this either matters or it does not. And as we do, let us be careful with each other, because someone in this room is not discussing this in the abstract.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, and if it does not feel resolved, that is honest, because the problem of evil does not resolve on a schedule and pretending otherwise would be a lie. Take this into your week. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if you are carrying a grief or a doubt or a suffering that feels too heavy to hold alone, please do not carry it alone, talk to me or to someone safe. If you are in real danger or despair, tell me tonight, before you leave, because you matter more than any study. Let me pray for us before we go, because this study practices what it teaches, and ends not in advice but in prayer. Thank you for the honesty it took to be in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and the refusal of cheap answers, and name plainly that this is the question that drives more people out of the faith than any other, and that this room is safe for it. Establish that asking the question is permitted.

Week 2: Session 1, The Question That Will Not Quiet, full discussion, stating the problem at full strength including Ivan Karamazov, with care to take the skeptic's objection seriously rather than defeating a straw version.
Week 3: Session 2, The God Who Permits, providence and the Joseph verdict, with extended time on the difference between God working good out of evil and the evil being secretly good.
Week 4: Session 3, Job and the Whirlwind, the book that refuses the formula, with extended time on the rebuke of the friends and on presence over explanation.
Week 5: Session 4, part one, The Crucified God, the cross as God's entry into suffering, sitting first with the cry of dereliction and what it means that God prayed the why.
Week 6: Session 4 continued, the Bonhoeffer witness and the skeptic's reply that a suffering God is only sympathy, drawing out that the cross is followed by the empty tomb.
Week 7: Session 5, Hope That Does Not Disappoint, the resurrection and new creation, suffering defeated rather than explained, handled with care so the hope does not minimize the grief.

Week 8: Integration. Trace the whole movement, question to providence to Job to cross to hope, revisit the five practices, and name what each person is carrying, with space and a clear path to further help for anyone needing it.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the question at full strength and the doctrine of providence, the problem stated and the God who permits what he hates.
Week 2: Session 3, Job and the Whirlwind, the refusal of the formula and presence over explanation, with extended time on the rebuke of the friends.
Week 3: Session 4, The Crucified God, the cross as God's own entry into suffering, the center of the study, with the Bonhoeffer witness.
Week 4: Session 5, Hope That Does Not Disappoint, the resurrection and new creation, plus a short close holding grief and hope together.
