bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Written from inside Lewis's own bereavement after his wife's death, refusing the tidy answers he had earlier offered, a model of honest grief that does not resolve neatly. Supports the study's refusal of cheap comfort across all sessions.

bibliography.title: Where Is God When It Hurts
bibliography.author: Philip Yancey
bibliography.note: A pastoral treatment of the problem of suffering accessible to ordinary readers, holding the question honestly without pretending to a tidy solution. Useful companion reading across the study. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: The Reason for God
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Includes a careful chapter on suffering and the problem of evil written toward the skeptic, granting the force of the objection while pointing to the cross and resurrection. Pastorally aligned with the study's posture toward the doubter. Leader to confirm specifics.

bibliography.title: Walking with God through Pain and Suffering
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: A fuller treatment drawing together the philosophical, biblical, and pastoral dimensions of suffering, useful for leaders wanting more depth on providence and the cross. Offered as a deepening voice, not a substitute for the study's own line.

bibliography.title: The Crucified God
bibliography.author: Jürgen Moltmann
bibliography.note: The most influential modern statement of the theology of divine suffering, arguing that the cross reveals a God who takes pain into his own life. Background for session 4 and the contested question of divine impassibility. Offered as one serious voice in a debate, not as settled doctrine.

bibliography.title: God, Freedom, and Evil
bibliography.author: Alvin Plantinga
bibliography.note: The philosophical case widely held to show that there is no strict logical contradiction between an all-good, all-powerful God and the existence of evil, shifting the debate to the evidential and existential form. Background for the goingDeeper of session 1.

bibliography.title: The Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The source of the account of evil as the privation of good, a corruption of what God made rather than a thing in itself, and of the restless heart that finds rest only in God. Background for the nature of evil discussed across the study.

bibliography.title: Lament for a Son
bibliography.author: Nicholas Wolterstorff
bibliography.note: A philosopher's raw, unresolved grief after the death of his son, refusing easy comfort and holding faith and anguish together. A model of the honesty the study aims for, useful especially alongside session 5. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as the study's own.

bibliography.title: The Doors of the Sea: Where Was God in the Tsunami
bibliography.author: David Bentley Hart
bibliography.note: A sharp theological argument against making God the author of evil, written in response to a natural disaster, insisting that God is at war with suffering rather than its cause. Offered as a serious voice on providence in session 2, to be weighed rather than simply adopted.

furtherReading: The Brothers Karamazov, Fyodor Dostoevsky, for readers willing to meet the problem of evil at its most honest, in Ivan's refusal of a harmony bought with a child's tears, read alongside the study's first session.

Letters and Papers from Prison, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for those who want to sit with the witness of a man who found in the suffering God his only help while facing execution, the heart of the study's fourth session.
A Grief Observed, C. S. Lewis, for anyone living inside a grief that does not resolve, written from the middle of it and refusing the tidy answers, a companion for the whole study.

Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, Timothy Keller, for readers who want a fuller treatment holding the philosophical, biblical, and pastoral threads together, leader to confirm specific claims.
Where Is God When It Hurts, Philip Yancey, for those who want a pastoral and accessible companion to the question, honest about the difficulty without pretending to a solution.

glossary.definition: The ancient and central objection that a God who is both all-good and all-powerful seems incompatible with the existence of real and terrible suffering. The study takes it at full strength and refuses every answer that dissolves it by quietly dropping one of those three claims.

An attempt to justify the goodness and power of God in the face of evil. The study is wary of theodicies that explain suffering away, insisting that Scripture's deepest response is not an explanation but the presence of a God who entered the suffering himself.

The doctrine that God governs all things, permitting what he hates and bending even genuine evil toward an end its author never intended, as in Joseph's verdict, without making the evil itself good or claiming we can read his purpose from inside our suffering.

The argument, associated with Alvin Plantinga, that there is no strict logical contradiction in an all-good, all-powerful God permitting evil that arises from the genuine freedom he grants his creatures, which shifts the debate from the logical to the evidential and existential form.

Jesus' cry from the cross, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, the question of the suffering soul prayed by God in human flesh, which the study makes central to its claim that the why has been taken up into the heart of God.

The classical doctrine that God in his divine nature is not subject to suffering, held to protect that he is not a victim of forces greater than himself. The study notes the contested modern challenge to it and lands on the shared pastoral center, that in Christ God truly entered human suffering.

Augustine's account of evil not as a thing in itself but as a corruption or absence of the good God made, the way blindness is the loss of sight rather than a substance, which guards against treating evil as a rival creation alongside the good.

The biblical prayer of honest complaint and protest, how long O Lord, brought directly to God, which the study holds up as a permitted and even modeled form of faith, the cry of the afflicted that Scripture never rebukes.

The storm out of which God answers Job, not with an explanation of his suffering but with his presence and a flood of questions that relocate Job inside a creation too large for his own accounting, the study's image for presence over explanation.

The Christian claim, distinct from every god kept at a distance from pain, that God did not stay outside human suffering but entered it fully on a cross, so that there is now no human pit God has not known from the inside.

The biblical hope of a renewed heaven and earth where God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear, where death and mourning and pain are no more, the study's final word on suffering as defeated rather than explained.

Christian hope grounded not in vague optimism but in the resurrection of Jesus as a claimed historical event, the assurance that suffering, real and unexplained, will finally be defeated rather than merely justified, distinct from the opiate the skeptic rightly rejects.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: If God is good, and God is able, why does he allow suffering. It is the oldest question and the hardest, the one that drives more people out of the faith than any other, and most studies answer it with a tidy formula that wounds the very people it means to help. This five-session study refuses the cheap answer. It takes the question at full strength, in the form the honest atheist gives it, and walks slowly toward the only response Scripture finally gives, which is not an argument but a God who entered the suffering himself, on a cross, and walked back out of the grave. It is written toward the skeptic first, honest about the doubt, careful with the grieving, and it never explains anyone's pain away. Built so any volunteer can lead it with no prep. Come honest, not finished.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We are starting a five-week study on the hardest question there is, where is God when it hurts, the problem of suffering and the goodness of God. Before anyone braces, hear this. It is not a study that will hand you a tidy answer to why God allows suffering, because there is not one, and it will not shame your doubt or explain away your grief. It takes the question seriously, the way an honest skeptic asks it, and it implicates the preacher first, because this exact question was the wall I could not climb for a long time. It is for the doubter, the griever, and the skeptic, and it walks toward a God who did not stay above the pain but entered it. No homework, and no prep needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.

quoteCards: I am not going to answer the problem of evil to your satisfaction, because if I could reduce the suffering of the world to a paragraph, that paragraph would be obscene.
The question is not the enemy of faith. The atheist returns his ticket and walks away. The believer returns his ticket and stays in the room.
Joseph looked at the brothers who sold him and called it evil to its face, and in the same breath said God meant it for good. He held both. He collapsed neither.
God was angry at the end of Job, not at the man who shook his fist, but at the friends who defended him with tidy theology.
God's answer to suffering was not an argument. It was a presence. He did not give Job a reason. He gave Job himself.
The cross does not explain your suffering. It tells you that whatever pit you are in, God has been there before you, not as a tourist but as one of the crucified.
On the cross, God in human flesh prayed the question of this whole study. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me.
The Christian hope is not that suffering made sense. It is that suffering, real and terrible and unexplained, is going to be defeated.
Not suffering explained. Suffering ended, wiped from every face by the hand of God himself.
The dark is real. I have not pretended otherwise. But the dark is not the last word. The last word is a morning, and a hand on a wet face.
